Troubleshooting

Symptom-first list of what breaks on this box: the error string, the cause, the recipe, and what the fix costs.

  • Knowing the cost of a fix before running it, including what it destroys

Deep, symptom-first list. The operational dev-stack/prod-stack, search-check and spark-verify targets are described in README.md and project-conventions.md.

Each fence below is one copy-paste action. A heading quotes the error string where there is one, so start with grep -n on the text you saw.

Placeholders: <wsid> is a workspace id and <ws> a workspace name. The workspace container is coder-<owner>-<ws> (so coder-alx-self-coder); the <wsid> form names the DinD

DinD

Docker-in-Docker — a workspace's own sidecar daemon, addressed through DOCKER_HOST.

 pieces around it - the sidecar coder-<wsid>-dind-sidecar, on the network coder-<wsid>-dind, with its own coder-<wsid>-dind-lib volume. What runs "from the stack host" needs a shell there: inside a workspace docker addresses that workspace's own private daemon through DOCKER_HOST=tcp://dind:2375, so a docker inspect aimed at the stack's coder or router container and run from inside a workspace queries the wrong daemon and answers no such container. bazelisk run //scripts:... also runs from the checkout.

Stack bring-up

not a directory: Are you trying to mount a directory onto a file -> missing compose bind-mount source

Cause: docker compose resolved ./proxy/homepage.conf (or another file bind mount) next to a compose file that did not have that file. Under bazelisk run that file used to be the runfiles copy, which only holds //:stack_data. Docker then created a directory at the source path and failed mounting it onto nginx's /etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf, which is a file in the image.

Fix: homepage/** and proxy/*.conf belong in //:stack_data, and the stack runners prefer BUILD_WORKSPACE_DIRECTORY (the real checkout) so relative mounts and bootstrap-issued proxy/certs/ resolve there. Re-run from the stack host:

The same command with dev-stack brings the dev project up. A leftover homepage-proxy container from the failed create is recreated on that up.

A failed bind from an older runfiles compose file can also leave a directory (or a root-owned file) at homepage/assets/icons/evo-t1.svg inside bazel-out/.../prod-stack.runfiles. The next bazelisk run then dies before the stack script starts; that spelling is the next heading.

FileAccessException / Permission denied on homepage/assets/icons/evo-t1.svg -> leftover runfiles bind-mount

Cause: an older bazelisk run used the runfiles copy of docker-compose.yml, so compose mounted ./homepage/assets/icons from bazel-out. Docker then created a directory where evo-t1.svg belongs, or the homepage container chowned those files to root. Bazel

Bazel

The hermetic build and test system every operator CLI is a target of.

 cannot recreate prod-stack.runfiles over that leftover, and the stack script never starts, so a repair inside prod-stack cannot help.

Fix: recover from a shell, then re-run. --repair uses sudo when chmod is not enough:

bazelisk run //scripts:prod-stack -- up is the command that pair recovers with; the make prod-stack-up (and make stack-up) shims run --repair before calling that same target. Bare bash scripts/setup-host.sh repairs leftovers and then installs any missing host tools. bash scripts/setup-host.sh --check lists leftover paths without writing.

error: .../.env not found from bazelisk run //scripts:dashboard-password -> the runfiles copy has no working .env

Cause: an older target ran the runfiles copy of the script, so $(dirname "$0")/.. was the runfiles tree, and that tree ships only //:stack_data. The working .env is untracked, so it exists only in the checkout, and the rotation reported a missing file on a host that had one. The path in the message tells the two apart: a bazel-out/.../dashboard-password.runfiles/... path is this entry. The same bug had pull-models pulling its default list instead of the checkout's OLLAMA_MODELS, coder-agents provisioning the compose placeholder LITELLM_MASTER_KEY instead of the checkout's, and spark-configure / spark-verify writing sparks/ output into a tree Bazel

Bazel

The hermetic build and test system every operator CLI is a target of.

 recreates.

Fix: those six CLIs (dashboard-password, pull-models, coder-agents, spark-verify, spark-configure, build-dev-image) resolve the checkout with resolve_checkout (scripts/lib/common.sh) before they read or write anything, so they honour REPO_ROOT and the BUILD_WORKSPACE_DIRECTORY that bazel run names. When nothing proves out - no candidate holds docker-compose.yml outside a bazel-out/, bazel-bin/, execroot/, or *.runfiles tree - the run exits 5 with one error: unresolvable repo root: ... line instead of half-running against a copy. Re-run from the stack host:

The first boot? run bazelisk run //scripts:bootstrap to create it hint alongside it means the checkout has no .env at all: that is the bootstrap path. DASHBOARD_ENV_FILE points the rotation at another file and exists for test harnesses; there is deliberately no flag for it, because a flag that names a file this CLI overwrites is one mistype away.

Could not resolve host: github.com -> Tailscale MagicDNS is the only nameserver

Cause: /etc/resolv.conf names only Tailscale

Tailscale

The private network the host assistant is reachable over besides the LAN.

 MagicDNS (100.100.100.100). Docker's iptables, and Kasm

Kasm

Workspaces that stream desktops from a privileged DinD container.

's privileged nested dockerd, can make that stub unreachable. When it is, every lookup dies, including github.com, so git pull over HTTPS fails. This is host DNS, not GitHub auth.

On Linux, bash scripts/setup-host.sh --repair writes /etc/systemd/resolved.conf.d/evo-t1-public-dns.conf (DNS=1.1.1.1 8.8.8.8), runs sudo tailscale set --accept-dns=false, and keeps MagicDNS for ts.net via resolvectl split-DNS. --check still writes nothing.

A checkout that does not yet contain that --repair (the usual case: git pull is already failing) needs the same commands by hand, then pull:

--check prints which nameservers are in play and whether github.com resolves. Other ways to keep a public resolver: add 1.1.1.1 / 8.8.8.8 as a global nameserver in the Tailscale

Tailscale

The private network the host assistant is reachable over besides the LAN.

 admin DNS page.

The same MagicDNS-only resolver is what makes Terraform inside the coder container SERVFAIL registry.terraform.io (127.0.0.11:53: server misbehaving). That spelling lives under "Terraform and the host coder CLI" below. Compose pins public resolvers on coder so a template push does not wait on this host fix.

Model lane: Spark, LiteLLM, the agent backends

./.env: line 188: qwen2.5-coder:14b: command not found from bazelisk run //scripts:pull-models -> the model list was being parsed as shell

Cause: that target used to read .env with . ./.env, so the shell parsed the operator's file as code. An unquoted value that holds a space is a variable prefix followed by a COMMAND, and set -e ended the run on that line before a single pull:

The word the shell says it cannot find is the second tag. The same read would also have executed anything written on a line of its own in that file, and it exported every other key there (LITELLM_MASTER_KEY included) into the environment of the docker exec calls.

Fix: the target now reads the one key it needs through env_get (scripts/lib/common.sh), which takes the line as text. Quoted and unquoted values behave the same, and nothing else in .env reaches the pull. A value that is not a model tag - a stray ;, a leftover quote, a trailing comment - is refused by name before the daemon is asked and before any of the ~35 GB download starts:

  • The ollama service is IPEX-LLM

     on the Arc 140T, not Ollama

    Ollama

    The model-serving API the local runtime speaks; reached only through LiteLLM.

     from a registry.
  • runners=[ipex_llm] in its logs is that GPU backend confirming itself.

Stable stack (prod-stack addresses the evo-t1-prod project by default; name --project-name evo-t1-coder-stack to read a stack brought up by hand under the checkout folder's own project name):

The same command aimed at the dev stack, so with dev-stack and its default project name (evo-t1-dev):

  • Flags are accepted before or after logs; --project-name and --tail move either way. Only logs takes trailing service names, and here that trailing word is the service to read.

Grok agent mode makes no tool calls (it narrates and stops) -> an Arc alias served it

Cause: no Spark box was reachable, so the Arc answered, and the Arc path returns tool calls as plain text.

  • Look at the dashboard's Agent backend card first: its per-box widgets go to error state while agent still answers.
  • Probe that endpoint. The card reads the same URL: AGENT_MODEL_URL from .env when it is set, and otherwise box 2 composed from SPARK2_HOST plus SPARK_HTTP_PORT, which is what spark-verify prints as spark2_openai in its --json facts:
  • Or check the whole fleet at once, from the checkout. spark-verify.sh takes --json and --no-tests; --no-tests skips the recipe's own probes (a 195k-token needle plus a 1/2/4/5-client sweep, minutes per box) and leaves the quick read-only check:
  • Its host list comes from SPARK_HOSTS in the process environment, then the SPARKn_HOST keys in .env, then the host part of SPARKn_OPENAI_URL - in that order, which is why the default run needs no arguments. With none of them set it falls back to the placeholders .env.sample ships, spark-1.lan spark-2.lan spark-3.lan, which do not resolve. Export SPARK_HOSTS="host1 host2 ..." only to check a fleet that .env does not name. A SPARKn_OLLAMA_URL left over in .env from the era when a Spark box served Ollama

    Ollama

    The model-serving API the local runtime speaks; reached only through LiteLLM.

     is no longer read, so the box it names is simply absent from the fleet; the run reports that itself with a warning: line that names the key and the host, and the fix is to name the box with SPARKn_HOST or SPARKn_OPENAI_URL, or drop the key. A host that does not answer is a skip, not a failure.

Fix, one of these:

  • Bring the TensorFold server up on the box. <host> is what .env names, and --apply writes the per-host override file that server runs:
  • Or repoint SPARK1_OPENAI_URL, SPARK2_OPENAI_URL and SPARK3_OPENAI_URL in .env at a tool-capable OpenAI-compatible endpoint, then restart the proxy so it re-reads them. The stack runners have no restart subcommand, so this one stays a direct compose call:
  • Either way keep SPARK_n_API_KEY non-empty: SPARK_1_API_KEY, SPARK_2_API_KEY, SPARK_3_API_KEY. An empty key fails every request inside the proxy before it ever reaches the box.
  • The agent -> coder fallback keeps chat answering while a Spark is down, which is exactly when tools disappear.

The TensorFold log is full of warnings, or resumed at 0 -> read the line shapes first

The server on each Spark box logs four shapes, and three of them are this stack's own traffic rather than anything wrong with the box. Read the shape before you reach for the box.

  • [tensorfold] done chatcmpl-... prompt=58 ... effort=xhigh tokens=16 finish=length followed by warning: a reply reached max_tokens while still thinking, so its content is empty: that is the LiteLLM

    LiteLLM

    The single OpenAI-compatible proxy in front of every model, local and remote.

     proxy's health check, not a user. At the pinned tag the proxy sends the deployment's whole litellm_params through a real acompletion, so the lane's baked reasoning_effort rides along, and it asks for the default health_check_max_tokens of 16. A thinking reply cannot finish its reasoning in 16 tokens, so it returns empty content and the server warns about it. The reply is a healthy 200 and the deployment stays in the pool.

  • info: prompt cache: 80693 tokens, resumed at 79747, kept 1; 12 states, 6289 MiB and 0 MiB spare of 6465 MiB (hits ..., evicted ...): the box is out of prompt-cache room. resumed at N is how much of the prompt it did not have to recompute, so a healthy conversation logs a number just under tokens. resumed at 0 means it recomputed the whole prompt: something evicted that conversation's state. Watch evicted and the state count rather than any one line.

  • [tensorfold] ended chatcmpl-... reason=client-left prompt=... after=Ns: whoever asked hung up. A tiny prompt abandoned at around 81 s was a health check the proxy abandoned on its own probe budget; a huge prompt abandoned at around 400 s is a client with its own timeout, and it re-prefills from zero if it retries.

Two things on this stack cause the evictions, and both are tuned here rather than on the box:

  • Probe cadence. health_check_interval, health_check_concurrency and health_check_staleness_threshold in litellm/config.yaml decide how often every Spark deployment gets a real generation, and they ship at 120, 2, and 900 -- where the interval used to sit at LiteLLM

    LiteLLM

    The single OpenAI-compatible proxy in front of every model, local and remote.

    's own default of 300 s. 120 s is the floor the measurement allows, not a taste: at 30 s across five deployments a round was putting more probes on a box than user requests, and each one took a prompt-cache state from a conversation. A probe is a real completion -- the deployment's whole litellm_params through acompletion at the default health_check_max_tokens of 16 -- and the four probes queued behind a long turn were dropped by the proxy's own health-check timeout at about 81 s, which is the same reason=client-left shape as the line above. The cap itself is 60 s (HEALTH_CHECK_TIMEOUT_SECONDS, constants.py:1557), read per deployment (health_check.py:530), so the queue in front of the probe is the plain reading of the gap between that cap and the 81 s the log shows - the drop time is what was seen, the queue is inference. A box merely busy enough to stall a 16-token probe past that drop is what keeps the floor here: health_check_ignore_transient_errors: true is what now stops one slow 408 or 429 probe from also pulling that box off the fleet for a cycle (proxy_server.py:3971-3974, :4002-4006), but the probes still cost a prompt-cache state each, so nothing goes lower. Read the period as one sweep plus the interval, not as the interval: the loop sleeps after a sweep finishes, and a sweep is the 27 deployments that did not opt out through the concurrency-2 gate. If the warnings come back every few seconds, that interval is the first key to look at. What the filter those probes feed actually excludes, and what to check when it stops excluding, is under A Spark box is powered off and still getting traffic below.

  • The 195k needle. //scripts:spark-verify runs the recipe's needle.py --length 195000 as the window proof, and a 195k prompt the server has never seen is the largest single eviction on the box. It now skips itself while /health reports requests_running above zero, so it does not land on a box that is serving:

The window is still read passively on every run without the needle, from the server's own startup lines (context_pairs and startup_estimate in the report), so a box quietly rebuilt with a shorter window is still visible; the needle is the active confirmation of it. --no-tests skips all four recipe probes for a quick read-only pass, and that is what //scripts:bootstrap runs.

A Spark box is powered off and still getting traffic -> cooldown cannot see a refused connection, the health filter can

Cause: the exclusion people reach for for this is the one that cannot fire on the failure a down box actually raises. _is_cooldown_required returns False the moment the exception text contains APIConnectionError (litellm/router_utils/cooldown_handlers.py:223, ignored_strings), and a closed port, a dead engine process, and a TensorFold box that refuses with the status-less NoRoom value all surface as that exception. So no allowed_fails number and no cooldown_time cools a box that is simply gone -- which is why litellm/config.yaml ships no allowed_fails key at all, and why cooldown_time: 60 is there for the other failure: a box that answers HTTP and returns real 5xx.

Say which half of this entry is measured. The half that is: with enable_health_check_routing: true a box that answered HTTP 500 to client traffic received zero client requests in the sample window, against several with the flag removed and allowed_fails: 40 / cooldown_time: 5 restored - zero against several, from a throwaway three-box harness that a reviewer re-ran with its own containers. The refused-connection half, which is what this entry is named for, is read out of the two code paths above rather than measured: the harness's docker stop phase cannot show anything, because a stopped container logs nothing in either arm.

What pulls a down box out is the health filter, and it needs both halves of it running:

  • enable_health_check_routing: true in general_settings. Without it, _async_filter_health_check_unhealthy_deployments (router.py:14137) is a no-op at router.py:14153, and async_get_available_deployment (router.py:13041) hands least-busy the whole list.
  • A live probe loop: background_health_checks: true plus health_check_interval above zero. An interval that is unset or 0 returns from the loop before it starts (proxy_server.py:4071) and starves the state the filter reads. A router-wide allowed_fails_policy with background_health_check_model_groups unset switches the filter off a third time (router.py:14161), which is why no such policy sits in this config.

That is also why the picker needed the filter at all. least-busy raises its in-flight counter before the call and gives it back on the failure hook, and _least_busy returns the FIRST deployment at the minimum (router_strategy/least_busy.py:83, :120, :129, :143), so a box that refuses everything sits at zero and an unfiltered least-busy prefers it over a healthy box. "Off but still getting traffic" is the expected shape of routing with the filter off, not a bug to chase on the box.

Confirm it in this order:

  • Who does the router hold right now? GET /health with the master key answers it, and because background_health_checks: true ships here the handler returns the cached probe results (_health_endpoints.py:1218) rather than firing a fresh generation at every deployment -- an operator's read of this endpoint costs the fleet nothing. Each entry carries model_id, which is the per-box deployment id the config names (agent-spark-1, agent-swarm-spark-2, ...), plus api_base and exception_status, and the payload totals them as healthy_count / unhealthy_count. Narrow one box with ?model_id=agent-spark-2 or one lane with ?model=agent-swarm. On the stack host, with the LITELLM_MASTER_KEY the container itself runs with:

A box you know is off sitting in unhealthy_endpoints while its two siblings are in healthy_endpoints is the filter doing its job. It in healthy_endpoints too is most often the loop not running -- read the two general_settings keys above before you read the box. One innocent case is a restart or a redeploy of the proxy: no Redis is configured for this proxy, so the marks live in one process (router_utils/health_state_cache.py:32-36) and every restart clears them until the first sweep finishes, with nothing logged on the filter's fail-open exits. Right after a deploy healthy_endpoints can list a box you know is off; read /health again a cycle later before you conclude anything.

  • Is the process itself answering? /health/liveliness needs no key at all (_health_endpoints.py:1938), which is what the compose healthcheck: dials. /health is behind user_api_key_auth (_health_endpoints.py:1110), so it needs the master key and is not a liveness probe.

  • Do not read the proxy log for this. The probe loop writes its own lines through verbose_proxy_logger, so the sweep and the cooldowns it takes are DEBUG-level and a healthy-looking log proves nothing. The one line that does reach the default level is background_health_check_cycle_duration_exceeded_interval (proxy_server.py:4212-4214), a WARNING that fires when one sweep alone outruns health_check_interval -- it appeared in a measurement run with the interval at 15 s. Nothing in this repo measures the sweep at the shipped 120 s, so read the line as arithmetic rather than a settled all-clear: the sweep covers the 27 deployments that did not opt out, pushed through the concurrency-2 gate, so roughly 14 sequential rounds, and a mean probe over about 8 s crosses the interval. Treat it as a reason to raise the interval, not to chase the box. What 120 s does buy is that cycles cannot stack: the sleep sits after the sweep (proxy_server.py:4234) and concurrency 2 is a hard cap. bazelisk run //scripts:prod-stack -- logs --tail 200 litellm | grep -i 'cycle_duration_exceeded' is the grep worth typing; the loop's own lines need the proxy started with --detailed_debug.

  • /v1/models is not the read people try first: it lists the 13 model aliases, not the deployments under them, so a box that has been filtered out is invisible there and the alias still appears.

  • Is the filter still believing its state, or has it failed open? It returns the whole candidate list when the state is missing, when it is older than health_check_staleness_threshold, or when filtering would leave nothing to route to. That threshold is the fail-open window: at the shipped 900 s a deployment that drops out of the probe list altogether -- renamed, or removed from the config while the proxy keeps running -- is believed dead for at most 15 minutes and then takes traffic again. The vendor default is 600 s whatever the interval says, because it is computed from a constant (router.py:993), so the two keys move together or the filter fails open before the next sweep.

Then separate a sick proxy from a sick box, because each has its own fix. The litellm service carries a compose healthcheck: that dials the proxy's own unprotected /health/liveliness with the image's interpreter -- the image ships no curl and no wget -- every 30 s, with retries: 3 and a start_period: 60s that covers the config import and the 31 deployments built before uvicorn binds:

  • note: the daemon restarts a container that exits, and not one that goes unhealthy. restart: unless-stopped is what recovers a crashed proxy; the probe buys visibility ((unhealthy) in status and in ps, the last three probes in docker inspect, the event Alloy ships to Loki) and a service_healthy wait nothing here takes -- hermes deliberately keeps condition: service_started, because compose waits indefinitely for a healthy condition and a probe that stops passing would hold the host assistant down with the proxy.
  • ok: liveliness answering I'm alive! with no container unhealthy anywhere means the proxy is fine and the reads above are the ones to believe. A box that answers /v1/models on its own port is still not a box the router will use, and that distinction is what //scripts:spark-verify settles, from the stack host:

Recovery needs no operator action once the box answers again: the next green probe overwrites the mark with is_healthy: True (health_check.py:683), and the same loop is what notices, so a box that comes back on its own is eligible again inside roughly one sweep plus health_check_interval. Eligible is the precise word: the cooldown entry that same loop wrote for the box has to expire on its own (cooldown_time), and every failing cycle re-arms it, so the first turn back can still land on another box. What an operator does do is fix the box -- power, the TensorFold server, bazelisk run //scripts:spark-configure -- <host> --apply -- or, when the container is the sick half, restart it so it re-reads the config:

While every Spark is unreachable the agent group hops to coder on the Arc, which is why a fleet that answers at all can still be answering badly; see the fallback chain in docs/litellm-routing.md.

Sessions log compact failed: exceeded wall-clock budget 300s (runaway generation) -> a compaction stream that never sent a token, bought three times

Cause: the auto-compaction summary hung before its first token and nothing abandoned it. The CLI's 300 s wall-clock budget does not abort a call in flight - it is evaluated only after the response returns - so at 300 s its entire effect was to reject a summary that had already streamed in and make the session generate it again. Meanwhile the proxy re-dispatched every hung attempt to the same session-pinned Spark box, so one hang cost up to three request_timeout periods. Both halves are fixed here.

  • Prove recurrence before you touch anything. The events are in each session's updates.jsonl, so one pass over the store counts attempts against outcomes. The store rides the owner's grok-sessions-<owner-id> volume (shared mode), so run it where the sessions are (inside a workspace), and leave the ~/.grok/sessions path %-escaped as the CLI wrote it:

Read auto_compact_failed against auto_compact_started. Over the 11-day window this was investigated, the store held 82 failures across 15 sessions in 3 workspaces, escalating from a 39 per cent failure rate to 85 per cent (45 attempts in one day, 19 of them in the worst single session), and 3 of the 15 sessions ended on a dangling auto_compact_started and were abandoned.

  • Which sessions, worst first, with the same head cap so a busy store stays readable:

Each link in the chain, measured:

  • Auto-compaction always fired at about 75 per cent of the 262144-token window, the setting in force when this was measured: all 124 auto_compact_started events carried tokens_used between 196,636 and 214,585. Both template twins now ship [session] auto_compact_threshold_percent at 70, so a future sweep measures the events firing at a lower point than this.
  • The summary call rides the session model, the agent* thinking family, and inherits its output ceiling: captured on the wire as max_tokens: 32768, alongside 25 tool schemas and the workspace's x-litellm-session-id affinity header. [models] session_summary is not that lane - it serves titles and the session recap.
  • In every one of the 79 wall-clock failures no first token ever arrived. Successful compactions do stream: their elapsed_ms spans 107 s to 1915 s, and 18 of the 36 ran past 300 s, which is the summary the budget was discarding.
  • Nothing on the client aborts the hang. signals.json reports inferenceIdleTimeouts at 0 or 1 across the failing sessions, and no hung call was ever cut off at the idle deadline, so inference_idle_timeout_secs (then 1200 s) is not on this path. The key now ships at 1800 s in both template twins, which does not put it on this path either: the CLI still does not apply it to compaction. Reproduced directly: with an upstream held open and no byte sent, the CLI was still waiting at 3000 s.
  • The only live bound was the proxy's request_timeout: 1200, multiplied by every attempt. Observed failure durations were 1366 s, about 2400 s and 3465 s - the deadline honoured once, twice and three times.
  • Those re-dispatches came from this repo's own config. At the pinned tag ghcr.io/berriai/litellm:v1.102.1 a stream that dies before its first chunk raises MidStreamFallbackError, which subclasses ServiceUnavailableError (litellm/exceptions.py:1114 at that tag), and get_num_retries_from_retry_policy walks the exception MRO most-specific first, so it lands on ServiceUnavailableErrorRetries and never reaches DefaultRetries. A hung request never cools the box either: cooldown hard-excludes any exception whose string contains APIConnectionError, and _deployment_ids_to_skip_on_retry only skips deployments that answered a non-retryable int status code. Under the workspace-wide x-litellm-session-id pin every attempt therefore returned to the same saturated box.

What the fix changed, and how to land it:

  • ServiceUnavailableErrorRetries is 0, not 2, on each of the nine Spark lanes (agent, agent-low, agent-medium, agent-xhigh, agent-swarm, agent-explore, agent-review, agent-xhigh-fast, agent-swarm-fast): one attempt for a dead stream, so a hung request is bounded at 1200 s instead of up to 3465 s. DefaultRetries: 2 is untouched on purpose - TensorFold's NoRoom refusal arrives as APIConnectionError, which is absent from _RETRIES_BY_EXCEPTION_TYPE, so that walk falls through to DefaultRetries and keeps its two attempts. The proxy reads the file at boot:
  • Both templates/*/main.tf twins carry GROK_COMPACTION_WALL_CLOCK_SECS = "1200" in the agent env merge, next to GROK_MAX_MCP_OUTPUT_BYTES. The CLI reads that budget from the environment only (resolver crates/codegen/xai-grok-shell/src/util/config/resolve/compaction.rs, remote-settings key compaction_wall_clock_budget_secs); no TOML table accepts it, so a line pasted into grok-config.toml is silently ignored, the same trap [mcp] max_output_bytes already documents. It is honoured: setting it to 1 makes /compact fail with exceeded wall-clock budget 1s. Push, then stop and start the workspace so the new agent env lands:

What it deliberately does not do:

  • It does not stop the upstream from hanging. It stops the hang being bought three times, and stops a finished summary being thrown away.
  • TimeoutErrorRetries: 0 would not help: the hang never becomes a litellm.Timeout.
  • ServiceUnavailableErrorRetries is the only one of the two that can be zeroed; zeroing DefaultRetries breaks the NoRoom contract above.
  • The lever, now pulled: [session] auto_compact_threshold_percent ships at 70 in both template twins, so auto-compaction fires near 183,500 tokens rather than the 197k-214k these events measured, and the ~200k-token summary input shrinks with it. The store shows no size threshold separating failure from success - the successes reach the same 197k-214k range - so this is a load reduction, not a proven cure. Re-run the first command above to measure whether the ratio moved.

A summary on agent-xhigh-fast or agent-swarm-fast still takes minutes -> the fast-compaction hop did not fire

Cause: the hop is a proxy behaviour, not a client one, and it needs four things true in the same moment. With any one of them false the summary rides a Spark box exactly as it did before these two aliases existed - the 107 s to 1915 s measured above - and that is the slow path, not a fault. The Grok Build CLI has no compaction-model key, so there is nothing client-side to point elsewhere: the alias the session started on is the whole decision, and [models] session_summary is still not the compaction lane (see the entry above). The decision lives in litellm/compaction_router.py, and the five EVO_T1_FAST_COMPACTION* knobs named below are read there and nowhere else.

Start with the proxy's own line for the call:

compaction router: moved a summary call from agent-xhigh-fast to compaction-fast is the hop firing, once per summary, onto the tier it landed on: EVO_T1_FAST_COMPACTION_TARGET for a summary within the guard (default compaction-fast, which degrades to agent-low then coder) or EVO_T1_FAST_COMPACTION_SPARK_TARGET for one above it (default agent-low). No line at all is one of these:

  • Not a fast lane. The hop is armed by the alias alone, so a session on agent, agent-xhigh or agent-swarm compacts on Spark by design. The groups allowed to hop are EVO_T1_FAST_COMPACTION_LANES, default agent-xhigh-fast,agent-swarm-fast.
  • The kill switch. EVO_T1_FAST_COMPACTION ships on, and 0, false, off or no stops the hop on every lane at once. A value that is none of those and none of 1, true, on, yes also leaves it off, with one compaction router: EVO_T1_FAST_COMPACTION=... is neither on nor off warning per distinct value: a typo'd off is read as off. Compose gives each of the five keys its default in docker-compose.yml, and the value in force is the one interpolated from the env file when the container was created, so a stack that was already up when someone set the key is still running the old one. Clear the key (or set it back to 1) and recreate: a restart keeps the old environment.
  • Not the summary call. The CLI appends its instruction as the last turn, and the hook reads it there: one of the two asks the CLI sends, from a user or system role, in a turn no longer than the instruction itself. It does not read the system prompt, which rides every turn of the session, so a rulebook that quotes the sentence cannot move an ordinary turn. A request that merely mentions one of the two asks is not a compaction call and stays on its lane.
  • Too big for the Arc, and the Spark tier was blanked. The estimate covers the whole request, the tool schemas included, and charges a base64 payload and a non-ASCII reply at their own denser rates rather than the prose rate; anything above EVO_T1_FAST_COMPACTION_INPUT_LIMIT (default 24000) goes to EVO_T1_FAST_COMPACTION_SPARK_TARGET rather than to the Arc: the Arc weights answer inside a 32k window and Ollama

    Ollama

    The model-serving API the local runtime speaks; reached only through LiteLLM.

     would clamp such an input rather than fail it. Raising that key does not open the Arc tier: the fork takes the smaller of the key and the max_input_tokens the target group declares in litellm/config.yaml, so EVO_T1_FAST_COMPACTION_INPUT_LIMIT=100000 still forks at 32768 and logs one compaction router: EVO_T1_FAST_COMPACTION_INPUT_LIMIT=100000 is above the 32768 tokens config.yaml declares for 'compaction-fast'; forking at the declared window instead. A target group that declares no max_input_tokens at all leaves the key whole, and says so once with compaction router: 'compaction-fast' declares no max_input_tokens in config.yaml; forking at EVO_T1_FAST_COMPACTION_INPUT_LIMIT alone - that line is the signal to go declare the window, because it is the one state where the fork can still hand an oversized summary to a model that reads it clamped. A shipped auto-compaction arrives near 183,500 tokens, so it is the Spark tier that answers it. Blank that key, or name the lane the call arrived on, and an oversized summary stays on its Spark lane at the lane's own thinking level - the pre-hop behaviour, and the one case where the 107 s to 1915 s above is the documented limit of the feature. A summary that comes back short of the history it should cover has one remaining path that explains it: with all three Sparks cooled, the fallback chains end at coder - agent-low: ["coder"] for the oversized tier, and the same for the pair's own chains - and that Arc group answers from an input Ollama

    Ollama

    The model-serving API the local runtime speaks; reached only through LiteLLM.

     clamps down to its 32k window. That is every Spark lane's standing last resort rather than a defect of the hop, and bazelisk run //scripts:prod-stack -- logs --tail 200 litellm carries the health lines for that window - the fallbacks: block of litellm/config.yaml is the map it followed. Blanking works only because compose passes that key as ${VAR-default}: the colon form substitutes its default for an empty value too, and the parked tier comes back.
  • The tier names a group nobody declared. Neither target is validated by LiteLLM

    LiteLLM

    The single OpenAI-compatible proxy in front of every model, local and remote.

    , so the hook checks both against the model_name: entries in litellm/config.yaml and refuses a name that is not among them, with one compaction router: target ... is no model group in config.yaml warning per call. A typo there therefore looks like a hop that never fires rather than a summary that hard-fails. grep -E '^ - model_name: ' litellm/config.yaml is the list of legal answers for both keys.

A summary that moved and still came back slowly is the fallback rather than the hop: each fast lane degrades to the lane it is the twin of (agent-xhigh-fast to agent-xhigh, agent-swarm-fast to agent-swarm), and a twin is not in the lane list, so a session that lost its own group to a cooldown takes its summary back to a Spark with it. That is the alias-health case further down this page.

Coder Agents chat refuses every prompt, or its model dropdown is empty -> no model config

Cause: that chat has no model config on this deployment, so there is nothing to route to.

  • First run this to see the plan, then run it again without the flag to apply it:

  • After a stack up, the seeder that runs it in the background keeps its output in ${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/coder-agents-seeder.log (the note: line names the path). A chat that never got wired usually means that file holds a skipped: line: no coder container yet, no db container, or nobody had registered when the stack came up. Re-run the command above once the stack is up and somebody has signed in.

  • It skips while the coder or db container is down, or nobody has registered yet, and re-running it repairs a provider that drifted and moves a model pin whose alias has since gone unhealthy.

  • The closing summary counts the auxiliary lanes that carry a pin. A warning: naming a lane means that lane falls back to Coder

    Coder

    The control plane: provisions one Docker container per workspace over the host Docker socket.

    's own pick, and title_generation and compaction are the two an operator notices first: conversations stop getting titles, then a long one stops at the compaction threshold. Re-run --apply once the alias behind that lane answers.

  • A warning: that a stored model config is disabled, is not the default, or compacts against the wrong window names a row this script found already in place. It reads before it writes and this surface has no PATCH, so the correction is the one click in Admin -> Experiments -> Agent Chat the line names.

A chat that starts but narrates instead of calling tools is the no-Spark case above.

Coder Agents offers a model that errors, or a chat never gets a title -> an alias with no healthy deployment

Cause: the LiteLLM

LiteLLM

The single OpenAI-compatible proxy in front of every model, local and remote.

 alias behind that model has no deployment the router will use. The Arc aliases (chat, coder, coder-fast) go unhealthy the moment their weights are not in the IPEX-LLM

IPEX-LLM

Intel's XPU runtime that puts the models on the Arc 140T iGPU.

 container, which answers model "..." not found, try pulling it first, and the Spark agent aliases go unhealthy when no box answers.

  • //scripts:coder-agents reads that same health view before it registers anything, so once the weights are back, re-running it registers the alias and takes the compaction / title_generation pins off it. A warning: line names the alias it refused to register, and the closing summary: counts the warnings, so a run that quietly wired half the model list is visible.
  • Titles that never appear and a long chat that dies at its context budget are the helper lanes pointing at a dead alias. Re-running the script moves them.

Workspace cannot reach LiteLLM -> CODER_ACCESS_URL, or host.docker.internal

One lane reaches that port: a process inside the workspace. The two reads that matter are the probe from inside the workspace and the liveliness probe from the stack host, and those share nothing but the destination.

  • The model lane: a process inside the workspace dials http://host.docker.internal:4000/v1 directly. host.docker.internal is the docker bridge gateway (172.17.0.1), compose publishes the proxy's container port 4000 on host port 4000, and nothing between the two authenticates. LITELLM_BASE_URL and the coding CLIs use this lane.
  • The agent bar keeps :4000 off its own path: the workspace page's litellm tile is coder_metadata text (value = var.litellm_url), a read-out rather than a coder_app, so litellm-gmktecbeast. is never consulted here. Health-check the proxy with curl http://host.docker.internal:4000/health/liveliness on the stack host. The app lane under A workspace app link answers Bad Gateway below is the VS Code Web editor link and stays on 13337 inside the workspace.

The checks that apply:

  • CODER_ACCESS_URL must be an https:// URL: a LAN IP, or the public coder name in public mode. Never localhost and never 127.0.0.1.
  • The workspace container must resolve host.docker.internal; the model lane reaches LiteLLM

    LiteLLM

    The single OpenAI-compatible proxy in front of every model, local and remote.

     through that host gateway, and so does LITELLM_BASE_URL.
  • Agent traffic ignores that URL and dials host.docker.internal:3002; see the coder_agent_url template variable.

Search never answers (or answers empty) -> prove the search lane before blaming the MCP hop

The self-hosted SearXNG

SearXNG

The keyless metasearch lane that answers the agent's web searches.

 MCP stdio server is the search lane, declared by default (search_mcp defaults to true). Grok's native web_search is parked: the render sets disable_web_search = true, because no model transport this box ships serves that tool type - LiteLLM

LiteLLM

The single OpenAI-compatible proxy in front of every model, local and remote.

's agent group answers tools of type 'web_search' are not supported: this server runs function tools only (HTTP 400) before anything is fetched, and supports_backend_search = false does not route around it. An agent that still spends a turn on a native search call and comes back with that message behaved as configured; there is no native lane to fall back to. Two probes split a SearXNG

SearXNG

The keyless metasearch lane that answers the agent's web searches.

 fault in half:

  • bazelisk run //scripts:search-check (or scripts/search-check.sh from a shell that can reach the host gateway) dials the service directly. It reads $SEARXNG_URL before its http://127.0.0.1:8181 default, and every workspace's agent env carries that key, so a workspace-side probe needs no --url. It separates engines that answered, engines that were unresponsive, and an empty result page, and it names each engine the instance has parked together with the reason the backend gave (parked by its backend: google: access denied). A park expires after search.suspended_times in searxng/settings.yml, so re-run before writing an engine off. --json adds engines_parked for a dashboard to trend.
  • An agent whose searches come back empty while the service answers 200 is nearly always parked engines rather than a broken deployment: the general-purpose engines are the ones the public backends bot-wall first. The same query without an engines pin usually still returns results, which is why the guidance in ~/.grok/AGENTS.md tells an agent to leave the engine choice to the instance.
  • grok mcp doctor searxng inside the workspace probes the MCP hop. A healthy search-check plus a failed handshake points at the server, the URL or the port.
  • bazelisk run //scripts:mcp-check covers both hops plus the config side in one pass: the declared lanes, whether each command= binary is there, whether ~/.grok/config.toml is still stack-managed, whether the lane's credential is set, whether the search lane returns results for a plain lookup rather than just an HTTP 200, and each server's handshake. A missing binary prints the exact npm i -g --prefix /opt/npm-global command that puts it back.

There is no second lane behind this one, so run these probes before touching anything else. A service that answers but a server that will not handshake is the MCP hop; a server that cannot launch at all usually means no /opt/npm-global/bin/searxng-mcp-server, and that binary is baked into the golden image - an image that predates it needs a rebuild and a workspace recreate, not a config edit. Park the lane with search_mcp = false on the next template push (SEARCH_MCP=false in .env applies it to every new workspace) when a session should have no search tool at all. To restore the native tool, flip disable_web_search to false in both template twins and re-push - only for an endpoint that really serves the tool, or the 400 comes straight back.

Context7 or GitHub tools missing in Grok Build -> parked MCP block, or a handshake with nothing to authenticate

The three MCP servers (github, context7, searxng) ship by default, so a lane missing from a session has one of three shapes: the block absent from the rendered config, the command= binary absent from the golden image

golden image

evo-t1-dev:latest, the image every workspace container is created from.

, or the credential absent. Run bazelisk run //scripts:mcp-check first - it reports the declared lanes, their binaries, their credentials and their handshake in one pass, and it names which shape you are in (an undeclared lane is a failure, a missing binary a warning). grok mcp doctor inside the workspace lists the declared servers and their handshake. A park is deliberate and looks like this: GITHUB_MCP=false / CONTEXT7_MCP=false / SEARCH_MCP=false in .env (relayed by push-template.sh) or --var github_mcp=false / --var context7_mcp=false / --var search_mcp=false on a template push. With none of those set, a missing block is a defect, not a park.

  • A missing [mcp_servers.github] or [mcp_servers.context7] in ~/.grok/config.toml means the last push passed --var ...=false, or the workspace started from an older template, or the file carries no stack marker at all (next bullet). No sibling can blank it: ~/.grok/config.toml is this workspace's own file, so an absent block is this workspace's own render, not another workspace's. Clear the gate and re-push, then re-materialize the file and restart the workspace so the managed config.toml re-renders. Two routes re-materialize it: bazelisk run //scripts:refresh-configs -- --container coder-<owner>-<ws> from the stack host, for a running workspace container, and bazelisk run //scripts:seed-dev-env -- --home <dir> for a host home (a laptop, CI, or the contributor container).
  • A declared server whose command= the box cannot find is image drift: the templates declare a binary the running image never got, because it predates the npm bake in images/dev/Dockerfile. Rebuild evo-t1-dev and recreate the workspace, or install the pinned package into the running box (npm i -g --prefix /opt/npm-global searxng-mcp-server@<pin>, the pins live in images/dev/tool-versions.env).
  • A ~/.grok/config.toml carrying neither the managed-by: evo-t1-coder-stack line nor the __evoT1Stack = true key is a file the stack stopped managing, so neither the startup script nor the seed writes it again and its default lanes never arrive. The usual cause is not a hand edit: grok mcp add persists its own settings by rewriting that file and deletes every comment line, which used to revoke stack ownership by itself. The TOML key is what survives that write, so a config rendered by the current templates keeps its marker through grok mcp add. Take the file over deliberately by removing both lines. To give it back: delete the file and restart the workspace, or re-materialize it with bazelisk run //scripts:seed-dev-env -- --force.
  • A declared github server that fails handshake: the owner has not connected GitHub External Auth

    External Auth

    Coder's GitHub OAuth login, the only GitHub credential this stack provisions.

    , so $GH_TOKEN is empty. Use the GitHub reauth app, then start a new Grok session.
  • A declared context7 server: an empty CONTEXT7_API_KEY is the shipped default and does not fail the handshake. With no value the server sends no Authorization header, so it handshakes and answers at the public rate limit, and only private libraries are out of reach. A key in .env plus a re-push fills the env. When a context7 handshake really fails the key is not the cause: run bazelisk run //scripts:mcp-check and it says which of the block, the binary, the cache config or the handshake is not OK.
  • No web_fetch either, and that is not a misconfiguration: features.web_fetch is on, but on a non-xAI model endpoint that tool runs only through toolset.web_fetch.proxy_endpoint and this stack sets none. Route a URL already in hand to searxng's fetch_content, anything else on the web to the searxng search tool, and a library, framework, CLI or setup question to context7 (resolve-library-id first, then query-docs on that id).
  • Discover live tool names with search_tool, then call use_tool with that schema. Do not hardcode MCP tool names from memory.

A workspace app link answers Bad Gateway -> find who answered

The VS Code Web button is the one app this stack still proxies: its URL is /@<owner>/<ws>.<agent>/apps/code-server on the coder hostname, because coder_app.code_server sets subdomain = false. So a failing app link is an app-lane failure, and a 200 from litellm-gmktecbeast. is not evidence about it.

Two hops can answer 502 on that path: this box's nginx, when coder:3000 will not resolve or connect, and Coder

Coder

The control plane: provisions one Docker container per workspace over the host Docker socket.

's own Go proxy, whose ReverseProxy ErrorHandler fires when the app upstream answers nothing. Two reads tell them apart, both from the stack host:

  • A hit in the first means Coder

    Coder

    The control plane: provisions one Docker container per workspace over the host Docker socket.

     tried the upstream and gave up, so the fault sits on this box: check the devcontainer or workspace container first, then DOCKER_HOST.
  • X-Coder-Request-Id on the response, beside X-Coder-Build-Version, means Coder

    Coder

    The control plane: provisions one Docker container per workspace over the host Docker socket.

    's own Go proxy answered, so Traefik

    Traefik

    The reverse proxy that terminates TLS for the public names.

     and Cloudflare let the request through and the fault sits behind them. Nothing on this box sets Via or CF-RAY.
  • X-Evo-Proxy names the server_name that matched here: coder, litellm, kasm, homepage or hermes. Its absence means the request never reached this box's nginx.
  • Neither header, and a Server: cloudflare with a cf-ray instead: Traefik

    Traefik

    The reverse proxy that terminates TLS for the public names.

     or Cloudflare answered, and there is nothing on this box to read.

To take the same reading from inside the workspace, replay the path on :8080, the published router port. That reaches coder:3000 through the sidecar while bypassing Traefik

Traefik

The reverse proxy that terminates TLS for the public names.

, Authelia

Authelia

The authentication gate in front of the public subdomains, on the other machine.

 and the WAN, so a reply there that differs from the browser's https:// URL names the cloud hops.

--noproxy '*' matters: with a proxy set in the environment curl hands the name to the proxy instead of resolving it, and 000 or a 5xx then describes the proxy.

  • 000 on the first probe means nothing listened on 4000. A 200 application/json means LiteLLM

    LiteLLM

    The single OpenAI-compatible proxy in front of every model, local and remote.

     answered, so the model lane is healthy and the app lane failed somewhere else.
  • 000 on the second probe means the private lane is down as well, so the public failure is not a cloud-side one. 421 means the Host header matched no server_name here, which is what a rewritten Host looks like. STACK_ROUTER_CONF in .env names the conf those server_name lines live in; the vhost side of it is in UI and logins.
  • A 404 is what this stack answers for an unknown app slug or an agent that is not Connected; the agent is the text after the first . in <ws>.<agent>.
  • Signed into Authelia

    Authelia

    The authentication gate in front of the public subdomains, on the other machine.

     with the link still failing puts the fault behind Authelia

    Authelia

    The authentication gate in front of the public subdomains, on the other machine.

    : the app path is gated by the same policy as the rest of the coder name.

Workspaces: startup, images, the toolchain inside them

Workspace stuck in starting -> startup is blocking

  • startup_script is blocking by design, so a failure there surfaces as a failed build with the reason in the workspace startup log. The container is not marked healthy until the toolchain is staged.

How do I read the workspace start log? -> the body header, the last stage line, and the truncated tail

  • Where it is: open the workspace in the Coder

    Coder

    The control plane: provisions one Docker container per workspace over the host Docker socket.

     UI and read its start log, and from a host shell the same text is coder logs <workspace>. The agent's startup_script output is the body of that log, and each coder_script prints under the name Coder

    Coder

    The control plane: provisions one Docker container per workspace over the host Docker socket.

     labels it with - Seed the Grok Build rulebook, Seed the fleet agents, personas and skills, Fetch stack secrets from Infisical, and the rest, which are the display_name values at templates/workspace/main.tf:731-1015.
  • Every body speaks the same shapes (templates/common/boot-log.lib.sh, handed to each body as the boot_log_lib key of its templatefile() map):
  • Which body failed: the == <body>: start == header names it, and that name is boot_begin's first argument rather than the file's. The eleven in the shipped workspace twin are workspace startup (templates/workspace/startup.sh.tftpl:19), code-server, agents seed, stack skills, repo skills, stack fleet, stack advisors, stack hooks, terminal launchers, github token refresh, and infisical secrets; devcontainer adds dind bootstrap.
  • Which stage it died in: the last == <body>: stage i/N: <title> == line above the failure. On every path that got past its header a body's final act is boot_summary, so a body that printed a header and no closing summary: never reached the end of its own script - it died in the stage that line names, or Coder

    Coder

    The control plane: provisions one Docker container per workspace over the host Docker socket.

     stopped it at the script's timeout. The startup body's eight stage titles (workspace startup stages 1-8, templates/workspace/startup.sh.tftpl:37-326) are the map for anything about tmux, the CLI, the shell profile, the skills and the notes library, the editor settings, the Grok profile, ownership and the git credentials, or the repositories.
  • The one case where a body prints nothing at all and nothing is wrong: the vault body leaves before it opens its run when the image carries no infisical binary (templates/common/infisical-secrets.sh.tftpl:15), which is silent by design because the vault is optional.
  • A log that stops mid-boot is a spent budget, not lost scrollback. One agent's whole stream - startup_script plus every coder_script on it - is 1 MiB, a Postgres check on workspace_agents.logs_length (dump.sql, v2.36.6). When it fills the agent's uploader drops the NEWEST lines (codersdk/agentsdk/logs.go, maxBytesQueued = 1048576, the log queue full; truncating new logs path), and once the server answers LogLimitExceeded: true nothing further is uploaded. So the head of the boot survives and the tail is what you lost: read from the top, and treat a body whose summary: is missing at the bottom of the log as unproven rather than as a failure - it may have finished after the budget ran out.
  • Nothing raises that budget from here, and the loud fix is the wrong one: coder_agent in the provider this stack pins (~> 2.18, locked 2.18.0 in templates/workspace/.terraform.lock.hcl) takes no log-size argument, terraform plan answering An argument named "log_buffer_size" is not expected here., and the agent-side constant is not read from the environment. The bound and the about-40-lines-per-body writing rule it forces are in coder-templates.md.

Image missing tools, or the build aborts mid-layer -> curl: (22)

  • Cause: a pinned download returned an error. The layer prints curl: (22) and stops rather than shipping a partial image.
  • Fix: check that version in images/dev/tool-versions.env against the upstream release, then rebuild the image.

grok -> command not found inside a workspace -> the CLI was never installed

Cause: that container started before the CLI was baked into the image, or its start-time download failed.

  • Both of these answer nothing in that case; the first is the one to type:
  • The same probe in the other spelling: test -x ~/.grok/bin/grok.
  • /tmp/coder-startup-script.log holds exactly one curl: (28) line when the start-time download was what failed.
  • One-off fix, from the stack host:
  • Then open a new terminal; PATH there already includes ~/.grok/bin.
  • Permanent fix: rebuild the image and the workspace, which then starts from the image's own copy. See the next two entries for the command.

A stack skill command missing from Grok Build on code-server web -> the stack's own seed is what provides it

Covers all six stack-shipped skill commands: /ez-learn, /ez-skillify, /ez-create-skill, /ez-bazel-first, /ez-strong-types and /ez-trunk-based-repo. The diagnosis and the commands below are identical for each one; only the name changes, so read <name> as whichever of the six you are chasing. The last three are the repository-conversion family and ride coder_script.stack_repo_skills rather than coder_script.stack_skills, so a missing one of those points at that body's log.

Cause: no published source names an upstream /learn, so there is none to miss. The xai-org/grok-build built-in command table, all 240 pages of docs.x.ai, every first-party changelog under x.ai/cli/changelogs/, and the public xai-org/plugin-marketplace catalog all carry zero occurrences of it, so there is no published copy to vendor in. The memory family /ez-learn copies (/flush, /dream, /remember, /memory) is a different case: those are upstream commands the CLI ships itself - /flush, /dream and /memory are built-in registry entries gated behind cross-session memory, which is off by default here, and /remember is a pager command with no such gate. The CLI does download its bundled platform skills at runtime (GROK_SKILLS_BASE_URL, cli-chat-proxy.grok.com) and that route needs an x.ai sign-in: from a workspace api.x.ai answers 404 and cli-chat-proxy.grok.com answers 401 anonymously, and a session started with --sandbox off still leaves ~/.grok/bundled/ uncreated. LiteLLM

LiteLLM

The single OpenAI-compatible proxy in front of every model, local and remote.

 is the sole model transport here, there is no x.ai credential, and the fetch never runs. So each slash command this stack ships is its own seed, written at workspace start by coder_script.stack_skills into ~/.coder/skills/<name>/SKILL.md with a twin copy at ~/.agents/skills/<name>/SKILL.md, and a missing command means that seed is missing, not that the image is stale. Each carries its own ez- name to stay clear of the upstream names: a user-scope skill overrides a same-named bundled one, so a seed named create-skill would hide the CLI's bundled platform skill of that name on any CLI that does sign in.

  • An entry for <name> with userInvocable: true in the grok inspect --json output is the pass condition: the slash command exists on that CLI, and the Grok Build terminal profile shows it because that profile execs the same binary.
  • No <name> entry and both ls paths missing: the seed never landed, which means the workspace booted from templates pushed before the seed existed. Re-push the templates and restart the workspace, or reseed into the running container from the stack host: bazelisk run //scripts:refresh-configs -- --container coder-<owner>-<ws>.
  • One of the six missing from both homes while the others landed points at the one body that seeds it: coder_script.stack_skills carries the authoring trio and coder_script.stack_repo_skills carries the repository-conversion family. That script's own log is where its seed body ran or failed, and the body is silent on a healthy workspace, so an empty log with a missing file means the body did not run at all (restart the workspace and read that script's log). The trio moved out of startup.sh.tftpl into that one body, so a startup-script log that says nothing no longer covers it. A SKILL.md that is present while its scripts/*.py helper is missing is the same story on the helper's own absent guard: the family seeds six payloads, each guarded on its own path.
  • Both ls paths present but no <name> entry: the loader dropped the file. Frontmatter must start on line 1, so anything above the opening --- silently kills the skill.
  • A learn directory still listed by the last ls is a copy someone took over: the boot and the reseed delete that path only while it still carries the stack marker, and a marker-free file is user-owned, so it stays. A marker-carrying leftover is retired on the next boot or reseed, and that removal only finishes the rename: no published source names an upstream /learn for the name to free.
  • A file you deleted or edited on purpose is not a fault. To keep your own version, edit it and delete the managed-by: evo-t1-coder-stack marker line: a marker-free file is user-owned, and the seeder leaves it alone unless you pass --force. A deletion is undone - the workspace boot writes the file again whenever it is absent, and refresh-configs re-seeds an absent target, so the next boot restores the stack's copy. Copy the payload back from templates/common/<name>.SKILL.md to give the file back to the stack.
  • ls ~/.grok/bundled/skills printing nothing is the expected answer, not a symptom: without the sign-in there is no bundled cache at all, on any version. Because a user-scope skill overrides a same-named bundled one, and the built-in memory names are the CLI's, this stack's seeds deliberately carry ez- names; the boot and the reseed retire a marker-carrying skills/learn/SKILL.md that predates the rename rather than relying on you to delete it, since deleting a seeded copy would not retire the old command name anyway - the boot and the reseed write it again. What works: keep a marker-free local copy only if you also stop the stack from seeding it, or disable the lane with disabled = ["<name>"] under [skills] in ~/.grok/config.toml.
  • command -v grok answering ~/.grok/bin/grok is the normal answer, not a leftover installer copy: the workspace PATH lists ~/.grok/bin before /usr/local/bin, and that entry is a symlink into ~/.grok/downloads/, which holds one file per downloaded release and is where grok update installs - so moving it aside does not outlast the next self-update. Compare command -v grok and both --version outputs (~/.grok/bin/grok --version, /usr/local/bin/grok --version) against GROK_VERSION in images/dev/tool-versions.env: the profile copy follows grok update, the image copy follows the pin. Neither copy gates the three seeded commands, and the two disagreeing is never on its own a reason to rebuild the image.
  • A golden image

    golden image

    evo-t1-dev:latest, the image every workspace container is created from.

     that predates a pin bump reports an older /usr/local/bin/grok than GROK_VERSION (1.0.77 at the time of writing), and rebuilding images/dev (bazelisk run //scripts:build-dev-image) is the CLI upgrade path - but the seeded skill commands work on either CLI, so this symptom alone never justifies an image rebuild.
  • Pin notes and the seeding contract: grok-build-and-agents.md.

grok doctor flags voice.no-input-device or terminal.limited-color -> a headless container, and where you ran the command

Cause: both are properties of the environment. Neither points at a workspace that needs repair, and neither is fixable from inside the container.

  • voice.no-input-device: the container has no microphone and no recorder on PATH. The probe checks for a recorder binary, so installing alsa-utils makes Doctor answer available with nothing to record from; the image ships no recorder and the finding stays. The PulseAudio route that would make capture real: the voice bullet in grok-build-and-agents.md.
  • terminal.limited-color: a tool command spawned by a running Grok session inherits NO_COLOR=1. Rerun grok doctor from the terminal itself and the report reads color truecolor with themes all.
  • A tmux finding that survives a reseed of ~/.tmux.conf is a reload gap: a client reads terminal-features when it attaches. Run tmux source-file ~/.tmux.conf, detach, reattach, then tmux display -p '#{client_termfeatures}' and expect RGB and extkeys in the list.
  • terminal.ssh-wrap asks to be run on the workstation you type ssh on: grok doctor fix ssh-wrap there. Nothing a workspace installs satisfies it.

The terminal process "/bin/bash '-lc', 'exec "$HOME/.grok/bin/grok-build-terminal"'" terminated with exit code: 1 -> something closed the tmux session under the tab

  • Cause: the profile asks tmux questions before it hands the tab to anything, and tmux exits 1 whenever it refuses. When a running agent meets it, the usual cause is the agent's own cleanup sweep - tmux kill-server, tmux kill-session, pkill -f tmux - closing the session the agent is typing in. The tab's process is that session's client, so the command takes the agent, its tool call and the in-flight reply down together.
  • Other refusals answer with the same exit code: sessions should be nested with care (a TMUX the tab inherited), open terminal failed: not a terminal, and -c <dir> naming a directory that is gone.
  • What the seed does about it, in the payload itself: the profile creates its session detached and attaches in a second call, so the tab that brings the server up is not the one whose close can take a running agent with it; every control call is bounded by timeout; and a create or attach that still fails lands the tab in a plain login shell rather than in VS Code's terminated-process message. So the message above names tmux itself failing, not the profile's logic. Confirm with:
  • What the stack does about it: both config twins deny the self-teardown family, so an agent's kill-server, kill-session or pkill*tmux is refused before it runs. The [permission] bullets in grok-build-and-agents.md carry the whole list and what an agent uses instead.
  • Reaching a shell once the sessions are gone: the profile does it for you now, and the bash profile in the terminal dropdown remains the route that no helper mediates. Then reseed from a host shell (bazelisk run //scripts:update-configs -- workspace) and restart the workspace, which is what re-renders its ~/.grok/config.toml.

The terminal process "/bin/bash '-lc', 'exec "$HOME/.grok/bin/vscode-terminal-tmux"'" terminated with exit code: 127 -> the launcher was never written

  • 127 is the shell saying the file it was told to exec is not there. Both editor terminal profiles exec a launcher under ~/.grok/bin, and coder_script "terminal_launchers" (templates/common/terminal-launchers.sh.tftpl) is what writes those two files. The profile, tmux and the tab are all fine; the file is missing. The same message naming grok-build-terminal is this same fault in the other profile, and the one naming neither is the exit code 1 case above, where the file exists and tmux refuses.
  • Cause: the three per-owner Grok volumes mount under ~/.grok - grok-notes-<owner-id> at ~/.grok/notes, with the memory and sessions pair beside it - and the Docker daemon creates a bind mount's target path as root:root 755. Whenever those mount points are new, ~/.grok arrives owned by root and the workspace user cannot create anything in it. This is the same daemon behaviour the ~/.shared/vscode/settings.json entry covers one directory over.
  • Why the repair missed: the startup script does chown ~/.grok to the home owner, and nothing orders that before this body. On Coder

    Coder

    The control plane: provisions one Docker container per workspace over the host Docker socket.

     v2.36 the startup script and every run_on_start body fan out in one concurrent errgroup - ten bodies launched inside the same millisecond in the start log - so the seeds run first and meet a directory they cannot write. They then said nothing about it: mkdir -p ... 2>/dev/null swallowed the refusal, cat > failed, and the run printed ok: for each launcher and closed at summary: 2 ok, 0 warnings, 0 failed.
  • Read the start log before touching the profile. The same boot takes the rest of the ~/.grok family with it, because those bodies raced the same chown: ~/.grok/AGENTS.md, ~/.grok/agents/, ~/.grok/personas/ and ~/.grok/hooks/. An affected workspace is missing all of them at once, which is how to tell this from one payload that drifted.
  • What the seed does about it now: each body that writes under ~/.grok asks for its own directory through boot_ensure_dir (templates/common/boot-log.lib.sh), which creates it and takes back the ownership of each component that is not this boot's to write, and the launcher body reads its two files back and prints error: naming the 127 when one did not land. A boot that cannot write now says so in its own summary line.
  • Confirm with:

Then look at the == terminal launchers: start == run in the workspace start log and read its summary: line: a green 2 ok, 0 warnings, 0 failed with no files is the old template, and 3 failed with two error: lines is a boot that still cannot write.

  • Fix: push the templates from the stack host and restart the workspace - the bodies are template text, so a workspace on an older template version keeps the race.
  • To bring one workspace back while the restart waits, re-materialize the two files from a shell in it: bazelisk run //scripts:seed-dev-env -- --home "$HOME". The bash profile in the terminal dropdown stays the route no helper mediates.

docker -> command not found inside a workspace -> an older image, or the wrong preset

  • Cause: that container was built from an image predating the Docker client toolchain, or from the bare-Ubuntu Minimal shell preset.
  • Rebuild the image, then rebuild the workspace; the image is fixed at create time.

Permission denied / jq: error: Could not open file on ~/.shared/vscode/settings.json -> empty named volume is root-owned

Cause: Docker creates an empty named volume as root:root 755. The vscode-settings-<owner-id> volume is empty on first use (the image has no files there to copy in), so coder cannot write settings.json. jq and python then fail because the file was never created. already cloned, skipping on the next line is informational: the clone already exists.

Fix: the template chowns that volume (and the three per-owner state volumes shared mode mounts under ~/.grok) to the home owner before the seed, and skips jq/python when the write fails. Push the templates and restart the workspace; there is nothing to delete.

Grok profile missing in a fresh workspace -> startup already finished, so read the log

  • startup_script is blocking, so it finished before the agent reported ready and before code-server started. Check the workspace agent logs first.
  • Then run bash -lc 'command -v grok'. A workspace on a current image answers /usr/local/bin/grok, so an empty answer means the CLI is missing, not the profile.

E325: ATTENTION / Found a swap file by the name "~/.grok/.config.toml.swp" -> a vim the last workspace stop killed

  • ~/.grok/config.toml is a real file on this workspace's own home volume, so a swap file outlives a stop of that workspace and nothing else. The usual history is: someone opened the config in vim, the workspace was stopped with the editor still up, and the swap is now asking about a session whose container no longer exists.
  • Read the prompt's own lines before choosing. modified: no means it holds no unsaved work. The host name names the container whose vim wrote it, and each workspace renders its own config.toml now, so a name that is not this workspace's means the swap predates that split - it is left over from when ~/.grok was one whole-profile per-owner volume, which a current boot mounts read-only at ~/.grok-legacy for the one-time state copy and reads nowhere else. A name that is this workspace's own is the ordinary case: the home volume outlives every stop and recreate.
  • (D)elete it is the right answer for an orphan. Do not pick (R)ecover: every start re-renders config.toml from grok-config.toml.tftpl, so recovery would restore bytes the stack is going to replace regardless.
  • A current workspace clears these at boot by itself. grok_sweep_config_swaps in the agents-seed.sh.tftpl body moves a swap of that name into ~/.grok/stale-swaps/ once nothing in the container holds it open and it is over an hour old. The boot log prints the archived name, and vim -r on that path gets the bytes back for a month; the files in there are named sweep-...orphan... and only those names are ever pruned, so a file you put in that directory yourself stays. Two reasons the sweep may stay silent, both worth checking before you blame it: the config lost its stack marker, since the sweep deliberately stands down on an unmanaged config (grep -cE 'managed-by: evo-t1-coder-stack|__evoT1Stack = true' ~/.grok/config.toml answers it, and either spelling is enough; grok mcp add rewriting the file is the usual cause, and bazelisk run //scripts:seed-dev-env -- --force is the fix), or the workspace predates the body, which a bazelisk run //scripts:push-template and one restart settles.
  • The reason the prompt keeps coming back is that the file is being hand-edited at all. This workspace re-renders its own copy on every start, so an edit made there survives until that workspace restarts and touches no other workspace - no sibling's boot overwrites it any more. The keys live in the template instead: grok_subagent_max_concurrent, grok_subagents_lane, and grok_config_extra. docs/coder-templates.md#stale-editor-swap-files.

Only about 4 subagents run at once though [subagents] max_concurrent says 15 -> the writers are on a pinned lane

  • Read both halves of the rendered config, not just the width:

  • That first block prints two numbers now: the fleet's own ceiling as # fleet-width:, above this session's cap as max_concurrent (templates/workspace/grok-config.toml.tftpl:427-428, devcontainer twin templates/devcontainer/grok-config.toml.tftpl:428-429). 15 over 15 is this entry - the number is right and the placement is not. 15 over 4 is a different fault, where the width itself was set, and the rendered-width entry is the one that answers it.

  • max_concurrent is how many a session may have in flight. [subagents.models] is where each type's traffic goes, and a writer pinned to agent carries the workspace's own x-litellm-session-id, so the whole fan-out lands on the one Spark box that key resolves to. That box admits PARALLEL (5 by default, scripts/spark-configure.sh) full-length streams and the parent session holds one of them, which is why the useful width there is about 4 no matter what the number above it says. The rest queue: limit_behavior = "queue" holds the overflow rather than failing the spawn.

  • Read those same four lines for the depth, because the block now prints max_depth beside max_concurrent (templates/workspace/grok-config.toml.tftpl:428-429), rendered from the grok_subagent_max_depth variable whose default is 2. At 2 a child spawns read-only mappers of its own, so a wave can be wider than the parent's own slots, and each in-flight child holds one of the fleet's 15 streams: a parent sums 1 + spawns per task and keeps that total at or below the fleet's stream count, because a stream past 15 is refused by the box. At 1 nothing nests, which is the rollback.

  • A review panel that arrives one at a time is the same queueing. The panel is three skeptics dispatched in one turn - requirements, proof, adversary - each on agent-review, each owning no file, each allowed up to 3 read-only mappers of its own, and all of them want the fleet's streams at once. While writers are still in flight the panel waits behind them, so dispatch it once the writers have landed.

  • GROK_SUBAGENTS_MAX_DEPTH in the agent environment outranks what config.toml says, so a workspace that nests differently from its rendered config is carrying that key; env | grep GROK_SUBAGENTS names it.

  • The shipped default puts the writers on the unpinned agent-swarm lane, where the least-busy picker spreads them over every box and the 15 is the fleet's real width (3 boxes x PARALLEL 5). Four keys come from that one variable: general-purpose, implementer, documenter, tester. If those read agent, the template was pushed with --var grok_subagents_lane=agent, which is the documented rollback to one box.

  • First work out which producer wrote the file, because there are two and they take the lane from different places:

A ws-... value means Terraform rendered it; contributor means bazelisk run //scripts:seed-dev-env did, and that path takes the lane from the GROK_SUBAGENTS_LANE environment variable (scripts/seed-dev-env.sh), defaulting to agent-swarm, and the ceiling from GROK_SWARM_WIDTH (scripts/seed-dev-env.sh:185), so a contributor home carries the same pair.

  • On the Terraform path, no dotenv key, no CLI flag, and no //scripts:push-template passthrough names that variable, so it was set by a raw coder templates push --var grok_subagents_lane=.... Undo it the same way from the stack host, or by re-pushing once the default in templates/*/coder.tf is agent-swarm:
  • Restarting is not optional: the value is baked into the agent's startup script at push time, and update-configs deliberately never re-copies config.toml. docs/litellm-routing.md and docs/grok-build-and-agents.md#the-fan-out-seam.

The rendered width is below fleet-width

  • The profile carries two numbers and the gap between them is the diagnosis:

# fleet-width: is the fleet's own ceiling, max_concurrent this session's cap (templates/workspace/grok-config.toml.tftpl:427-428, devcontainer twin templates/devcontainer/grok-config.toml.tftpl:428-429). They stay two lines rather than one number because an explicit --var owns max_concurrent and never moves the ceiling. 15 over 4 is this entry; 15 over 15 is the pinned-lane entry above.

  • Nothing in this repo renders a 4. Both twins derive the width from the fleet - grok_subagent_max_concurrent = var.grok_subagent_max_concurrent != null ? var.grok_subagent_max_concurrent : var.grok_swarm_width (templates/workspace/main.tf:553, templates/devcontainer/main.tf:581) - and take the ceiling beside it from that same variable (templates/workspace/main.tf:558). Measured: terraform apply with the shipped defaults prints 15, and the same run with -var grok_subagent_max_concurrent=4 prints 4. So a rendered 4 is a number somebody set, and a 4 still there is one that outlived what set it.

  • It can sit in two places, and they clear differently:

    • the template, from a raw coder templates push --var grok_subagent_max_concurrent=4. //scripts:push-template passes no fan-out --var of its own - its only grok_* one is grok_profile_mode (scripts/push-template.sh:528) - so a template-level value is somebody's raw push, the same shape as the lane rollback above;
    • the workspace, from coder start <workspace> --parameter ..., from coder update <workspace> --parameter ..., or from the Variables tab in the dashboard. (coder start takes --parameter name=value; --var is a coder templates push flag and that pair has no --var to give it - on Coder

      Coder

      The control plane: provisions one Docker container per workspace over the host Docker socket.

       v2.36.6 coder start --help lists --parameter, --parameter-default, --rich-parameter-file, --use-parameter-defaults and --no-wait, and no --var.)
