A workspace value survives every template push and is re-applied on every start, which is how a number typed in for one experiment months ago still caps a fan-out today.

  • One command reads both numbers and names the case, from inside the workspace:

Its verdict for this fault (scripts/subagent-check.sh):

The note offers both remedies because the check cannot tell them apart from inside the container: a workspace value and a template version's default live in the same database on the host, and neither is readable over the agent token. The second run of the check is what settles it, which is why the note asks for it.

Two near-misses read differently on purpose. A profile whose [subagents] table is simply absent answers warning: no 'max_concurrent' line - this profile has no [subagents] table; restart the workspace to re-materialize, and a restart is the right order there. A table that lost only its width line answers warning: the [subagents] table carries no 'max_concurrent' line - a hand edit, which no restart undoes, because the render writes that line and a file the render still owns never loses it on its own. A profile that answers warning: no '# fleet-width:' line above max_concurrent - this profile predates it; restart the workspace to re-materialize has no ceiling to compare against yet, so that one is a restart too.

The whole surface, for a script or a CI step that wants the answer rather than the prose (--help prints the same):

  • The same finding arrives by itself at every start: the profile stage of the boot compares the two numbers right after re-materializing the config (boot_stage 6 "the Grok Build profile", templates/workspace/startup.sh.tftpl:224, the comparison at :259-271, same lines in the devcontainer twin) and prints through boot_note (templates/common/boot-log.lib.sh:51), so the workspace start log carries note: subagents width 4 is below the fleet's 15 - a value that outlived its template, unless you set it on purpose.

  • Remedy, from the stack host, in this order:

Every start re-renders config.toml from the template, so the push only clears a template-level value. When the number sits on the workspace, put the fleet's own width back there instead:

coder start takes --parameter name=value and has no --var; --var belongs to coder templates push, which is the command above. The start itself re-renders config.toml, so that one line is enough to see the number move; it is also one-shot, so clear the stored value with coder update <workspace> --parameter grok_subagent_max_concurrent=15 or the Variables tab, or the next start narrows it again. 15 is grok_swarm_width under the shipped recipe - 3 Spark boxes x PARALLEL 5 (scripts/spark-configure.sh:92) - so a smaller fleet changes both numbers with --var grok_swarm_width on the push rather than widening the session past what the boxes can hold.

  • A width under the ceiling is not always a fault: it is the queue an operator sets on purpose for a session whose writers ride a pinned lane, where one box's PARALLEL is the useful width. The check prints the same warning either way, so the question is what general-purpose names under [subagents.models], not how big the number is.

Docker-in-docker

Cannot connect to the Docker daemon at tcp://dind:2375 -> the sidecar, or DinD off

Cause: the sidecar is unhealthy, its image was never pulled, or the workspace was created with DinD

DinD

Docker-in-Docker — a workspace's own sidecar daemon, addressed through DOCKER_HOST.

 off.

  • DOCKER_HOST is injected per template, not per toggle. templates/workspace sets it only while the toggle is on; templates/devcontainer sets it always, because that template always provisions the sidecar and the devcontainer CLI has to reach its daemon either way. So a set DOCKER_HOST tells you the template; the docker-in-docker metadata tile tells you the state (the devcontainer template always reads on (tcp://dind:2375), the workspace one reads off when unset).
  • Three separate reads, from the stack host. The first prints unhealthy rather than an error when the daemon fails its own probe, and no such container when the workspace has no sidecar at all:
  • That probe only asks whether the daemon answers docker version. It says nothing about the workspace that used to reach it.

did not find docker image 'docker:29.8.1-dind' -> plan-time failure, not runtime

  • Cause: that image is not in the host's local image store, and Terraform never pulls it. The docker_image data source only inspects the store.
  • So the workspace build fails at plan time, before anything is created, and it prints in the workspace's build log rather than anywhere inside the workspace.
  • Fix with the docker pull above, or turn DinD

    DinD

    Docker-in-Docker — a workspace's own sidecar daemon, addressed through DOCKER_HOST.

     off for that workspace.

Terraform and the host coder CLI

lookup registry.terraform.io on 127.0.0.11:53: server misbehaving from push-template -> coder cannot reach the Terraform registry

  • Symptom: bazelisk run //scripts:push-template queues, then dies during "Initializing Terraform Directory". workspace cannot list versions for coder/coder and kreuzwerker/docker on registry.terraform.io; devcontainer cannot fetch module "devcontainers_cli" from registry.coder.com. Both lookups fail with dial tcp: lookup … on 127.0.0.11:53: server misbehaving. Coder

    Coder

    The control plane: provisions one Docker container per workspace over the host Docker socket.

     itself stays up; bazelisk run //scripts:prod-stack -- logs coder repeats the same Terraform lines.
  • Cause: provisionerd runs terraform init inside the coder container. Docker's embedded DNS (127.0.0.11) forwards names it does not know to the host resolver. When that resolver is Tailscale

    Tailscale

    The private network the host assistant is reachable over besides the LAN.

     MagicDNS only, or Docker/Kasm

    Kasm

    Workspaces that stream desktops from a privileged DinD container.

     iptables has made 100.100.100.100 unreachable from a container, every public lookup SERVFAILs. The host CLI is fine; only the provisioner job dies. The lockfile reuse lines (Reusing previous version from the dependency lock file) do not skip the registry: Terraform still fetches the discovery document.
  • Fix: docker-compose.yml sets dns: [1.1.1.1, 8.8.8.8] on the coder service (embedded DNS still answers db and other compose names). Both templates pin the same resolvers on the workspace and DinD

    DinD

    Docker-in-Docker — a workspace's own sidecar daemon, addressed through DOCKER_HOST.

     containers so a later git clone of github.com does not hit the same SERVFAIL. Recreate coder so the new upstreams apply, then push:

Host git pull still needs a public resolver beside MagicDNS when the host itself is MagicDNS-only (heading above; setup-host --repair on Linux). Existing workspaces pick up the container DNS on the next start after this template version is active.

pq: value too long for type character varying(256) from push-template -> editor icon data URL

  • Symptom: coder templates push plans, then dies during "Cleaning Up" with internal provisionerserver error: execute transaction: insert resource: insert agent app: upsert app: pq: value too long for type character varying(256). Coder

    Coder

    The control plane: provisions one Docker container per workspace over the host Docker socket.

     logs coder_app's id was unexpectedly empty and then that Postgres error at inserting template import job resource.
  • Cause: both templates inline templates/common/vscode-alt.svg as a data:image/svg+xml;base64 URL on coder_app.code_server. Coder

    Coder

    The control plane: provisions one Docker container per workspace over the host Docker socket.

     v2.36 stores workspace_apps.icon as varchar(256). A multi-kilobyte SVG produces a data URL thousands of characters long, and the insert fails. The provisioner reports it at insert agent app: upsert app.
  • Fix: the SVG is a compact ribbon whose data URL fits the column, and push-template rejects a too-large copy locally before talking to the server. Pull this commit onto the stack host and re-run:

Error: No configuration files from push-template -> runfiles symlinks in the tar

  • Symptom: both templates fail during "Detecting persistent resources" with Terraform initialized in an empty directory! / Error: No configuration files. Coder

    Coder

    The control plane: provisions one Docker container per workspace over the host Docker socket.

     logs unpacking source archive size_bytes=30720 (tens of KB, not the ~120 KB of real .tf / .tftpl contents).
  • Cause: bazelisk run executes from the runfiles tree, where templates/** are symlinks into the execroot. A tar that stores those links unpacks in the provisioner as dangling paths, so Terraform sees no .tf files. The two templates/common/ payloads still land (copied with cp, which follows links), which is why the archive is small rather than empty.
  • Fix: push-template now prefers BUILD_WORKSPACE_DIRECTORY (the live checkout) and stages with tar -h so the archive holds regular files. Pull this commit onto the stack host and re-run:

REPO_ROOT: unbound variable from push-template -> the size guard read an ambient root

  • Symptom: bazelisk run //scripts:push-template prints == Preflight == and == Variables ==, then aborts inside == Templates == with push-template.sh: line 740: REPO_ROOT: unbound variable and never prints a summary: line. Nothing was pushed.
  • Cause: startup_size_guard looks up a payload the twin does not keep beside its own main.tf under templates/common/, and it did that by reading an ambient REPO_ROOT. Nothing in scripts/ ever sets that variable: the checkout is the root the script resolved and cd'd into at startup. Under the script's own set -u the read aborts the run. It only fires for a template that inlines a canonical payload, which is why a twin carrying its own copy never showed it.
  • Fix: the guard measures against the resolved root, and a parser it cannot open is now a hard stop rather than a silent "everything fits". Pull this commit onto the stack host and re-run:

  • bazelisk run //scripts:push-template prints it because no lockfile is committed under templates/, and Coder

    The control plane: provisions one Docker container per workspace over the host Docker socket.

     pushes the directory without one.
  • Pin provider versions locally only if you want to, per template directory. The push goes ahead either way, and workspace and devcontainer are the two names:

Editor, credentials, the clone

Unexpanded count argument on block "coder_app.github_app_install" -> apps were gated on start_count

Cause: coder/preview warns when a coder_app count is not expanded at workspace-create preview. start_count is that value. The default is then assumed to be 1. The only coder_app carrying a count today is coder_app.github_app_install, and it counts on github_auth_id, which the preview does expand.

Fix: coder_app resources are not gated on start_count (scripts, metadata and the container still are). Push the templates; new creates stop showing the warning. Existing workspaces pick it up on the next update to the new template version.

bash: -c: line 32: syntax error near unexpected token '(' after "Running code-server in the background" -> HCL $$(( in the editor wait loop

Cause: Coder

Coder

The control plane: provisions one Docker container per workspace over the host Docker socket.

 runs every coder_script as bash -c. HCL heredocs in main.tf only escape $${name} to ${name}; $$(( is two literal dollars. The editor wait loop then becomes waited=<pid>((waited + 1)), which is the syntax error. The echo before the loop still prints. already cloned, skipping on the next line is the concurrent clone stage, not the failure.

Fix: the increment is waited=$((waited + 1)) (one dollar). Push the templates and restart so the editor script relaunches.

A template push stops in "Detecting persistent resources" with vars map does not contain key -> a body used the one-dollar brace form for a shell variable

Cause: templatefile() reads a single-dollar brace reference anywhere in a coder_script body as an interpolation - inside a shell comment or a for loop as readily as in a command - and the plan then asks the caller's map for a key main.tf never declares. Both twins fail at once, because both render the same body from templates/common/:

The message names the body and the position, which is the whole diagnosis: line 32 there is if [ -L "${evo_t1_root}" ]; then, a shell loop variable.

Fix: write the shell variable through the double-dollar escape, which renders back to the literal ${name} in the emitted script. The unbraced form ($name) needs no escape. The gate that refuses the one-dollar form is //tests:bats_tftpl_interpolation_test; name the offending body and line with:

VS Code Web opens /home/coder instead of the cloned repository -> last workspace won

Cause: path-based Coder

Coder

The control plane: provisions one Docker container per workspace over the host Docker socket.

 apps drop the ?folder= query before the browser sees it, and code-server restores the last opened workspace (often /home/coder). The clone itself is fine (already cloned, skipping is not a failure).

Fix: the inlined fork starts code-server with --ignore-last-opened and the clone folder as a positional argument (/home/coder/workspace/<repo> on the workspace template). Push the templates and restart so the editor process relaunches.

A copy from an app inside a tmux pane never reaches the laptop clipboard in VS Code Web -> the browser build drops OSC 52

Cause: an app inside the pane - vim's + register, anything that emits OSC 52 - pushes its copy out through the pane, set-clipboard on with allow-passthrough on forwards it, and code-server's terminal hands the escape to nobody. There is no setting for it: the shipped 4.145.0 registers no OSC 52 key, and upstream microsoft/vscode#318254 is open with two unmerged fixes. Over ssh from Ghostty, kitty, WezTerm or iTerm2 the same copy lands, which puts the drop in the browser and not in tmux.

Fix: there is nothing to turn on in tmux. Copy the text the way the rest of the tab does - a plain drag is the client's own highlight, because tmux asks for no mouse reporting (measured on the shipped tmux 3.4: an attach with mouse on writes ESC[?1000h, ESC[?1002h and ESC[?1006h to the client, one with it off writes none), and the settings seed's terminal.integrated.copyOnSelection: true puts that highlight on the machine clipboard with no chord (the headless harness on 4.145.0 recorded navigator.clipboard.writeText firing on a client selection, before this switch). Right-click pastes it back (terminal.integrated.rightClickBehavior: "copyPaste" pastes when nothing is selected) and middle-click pastes it too (middleClickBehavior pinned to "paste"). tmux keeps no buffer of its own, so Prefix-] is unbound and there is no tmux show-buffer to read: the machine clipboard is the only clipboard here. Prefix m is the wheel switch, not a copy route: one press hands the wheel to tmux for a long scroll, the next hands it back. Paste is Ctrl+Shift+V or right-click in a bash terminal and a tmux pane alike, and Ctrl+V is not a paste on a secure origin (the pane gets the \x16 byte). Both directions, and what a pane app may still do over ssh, are in Copy and paste between a tmux pane and the machine you type on.

  • Output already scrolled off the screen: Prefix-[ is a viewer, not a copier - walk up with k, PPage or Ctrl-u until the line is painted on the screen, select it with a client drag, then q. A selection made inside copy-mode is inert: every copy binding in copy-mode-vi is unbound, so nothing ends it.
  • Copy and paste both dead, in both directions, a drag included: read the next entry. This one is a pane-app-only symptom, and a broken origin breaks the editor's own chords too.
  • history-limit reads 100000 but a pane still forgets old output: tmux applies the option when the pane is created, so that pane keeps the limit it was born with. Open a new pane, or restart the server with tmux kill-server.

Copy and paste both do nothing in VS Code Web -> the page is not a secure context

Cause: the browser exposes navigator.clipboard to a secure context only, and Coder

Coder

The control plane: provisions one Docker container per workspace over the host Docker socket.

's LAN door is plain HTTP by default (CODER_ACCESS_URL is the LAN address). Opened that way the editor has no clipboard API to call, so right-click paste stops with VS Code's own toast - "This browser doesn't support the clipboard.readText API needed to trigger a paste, try Ctrl+V instead." - and Ctrl+Shift+V only works at all through the browser's native paste event. A Clipboard site permission that was once denied does the same damage on an https origin, and there VS Code answers NotAllowedError: Read permission denied.

Fix: open the editor on the TLS public name (the coder-<host>.<domain> door Traefik

Traefik

The reverse proxy that terminates TLS for the public names.

 holds a real certificate for) rather than http://<LAN-address>, and give the site Clipboard permission - Chrome: the lock icon in the address bar, Site settings, Clipboard, Allow. The templates are not the variable here: both doors serve the same payload, so a workspace that pastes on one URL and does not on the other is an origin problem. What still works on plain HTTP: copy with a drag - the selection is the client's own, since tmux asks for no mouse reporting, and copyOnSelection's document.execCommand('copy') fallback really lands - and paste with Ctrl+V, the browser's own paste event - which is exactly what VS Code's toast tells you to do.

VS Code Web tab in Chrome creeps to gigabytes, or freezes now and then -> every tab was another mirror of one pane

Cause: each client attached to a tmux session is a full xterm.js in its own Chrome tab re-parsing the same stream, each holding a line-slot array sized from terminal.integrated.scrollback, and each taking its own copy of the rendered stream out of the server - 16 mirrors of one pane pulled 78.7 MB through an 8 s window in which a single mirror pulled 4.9 MB. The server renders the pane once, so a mirror is paid for in the tab rather than in server CPU: those same 16 moved the server only from 420 ms to 630 ms. A client activating or resizing repaints the window's other clients as well.

All of that applies to a client actually being read. Measured on this workspace, 7 of 9 attached clients received 0 bytes over a 4 s window in which the pane produced 12858, because code-server's pty host keeps the pty open after the browser side of the tab goes away and nothing drains it any more; tmux stops feeding a client it cannot write to, which is why 15 such clients against the same flooding pane took the server only from 450 ms to 730 ms. What a ghost really costs is the reuse decision. It holds session_attached at 1, and that is the number the attach helper reads, so the folder pays a whole new session - another pane, another xterm.js, another history - for every later tab. Count the clients against the panes, and count what each one is taking in:

More clients than you have visible terminals means the tabs are mirrors, and a client whose #{client_written} stands still while its pane is busy is a tab whose browser side is already gone.

Fix: the seed keeps one pane per visible terminal, and both launchers sweep their own sessions for a client that has reported no activity past a 6 h grace before they read session_attached - EVO_TMUX_STALE_AFTER (seconds) moves the number. tmux 3.4 only lets you detach by the client's tty path (detach-client -t /dev/pts/N): it refuses a pid with can't find client and has no kill-client. vscode-terminal-tmux reattaches a folder's session only while nothing is attached to it, and opens a numbered sibling (vscode-<folder>-<hash>-2, -3, ...) beside live ones, so an extra tab is a new pane rather than a mirror. Every session target in that helper carries tmux's = exact-match prefix, because a bare name is also answered by any session starting with it - once foo is closed, foo-2 would otherwise answer for it and put a second client on a live pane. And when tmux 3.4 does take a session down under a tab that is reopening it, the helper raises a fresh one rather than letting the tab exit with it. The settings seed drops terminal.integrated.scrollback to 2000 - the browser keeps a short viewport and tmux's history-limit 100000 behind Prefix-[ holds the deep history - and turns cursorBlinking off, and templates/common/tmux.conf sets set -s escape-time 10 and set -g focus-events on. The first is the freeze: 3.4 holds back any Escape it reads for 500 ms to decide whether a sequence follows, so Alt and the arrow keys feel like dropped input and a focus-in can wait that long - twice, with set-timing - before tmux repaints. Upstream cut the default to 10 ms in 3.5, and 0 - the value vim guides suggest - is the one to avoid: measured on this build, a throttled tab that delivers Esc and the next character more than 10 ms apart loses its Alt chords, and 0 makes that far likelier. focus-events is what gives tmux a focused client to work with at all. aggressive-resize stays at its default on purpose: its own entry in options-table.c scopes it to the smallest and manual window-size modes, the shipped default is latest, and tmux(1) calls it "poor for interactive programs such as shells". Both files reseed on the next start only while they still carry the stack marker, so delete either one you edited by hand. Before debugging a setting that will not take: tmux reads ~/.tmux.conf and then $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/tmux/tmux.conf and ~/.config/tmux/tmux.conf, last file read wins, so either of those quietly outranks everything the seed writes. focus-events is read when a client attaches, so the tabs need to be gone for it to land: close them all after the restart and reopen one per pane.

  • If a tab keeps dying on you and you want to know whether the pane's shell exited or tmux took the session down under the tab, run tmux set -w remain-on-exit on in it first: the pane then stays on screen with its exit status in #{pane_dead_status} instead of vanishing, which is what the tmux FAQ recommends for exactly this question. Turn it back off afterwards - a dead pane is not yours to keep.

  • Residual: a tab you hide rather than close keeps its xterm instance alive and still buffers whatever the pane prints, and nothing in the stack caps that. Neither does tmux: 3.4 has no per-client output limit, and an ordinary attached client that stops draining its pty is never dropped (measured here: one stayed attached past 15 minutes while the server kept serving commands). The only "too far behind" disconnect is in control mode, behind a hardcoded 300 s age in control.c, which a VS Code tab never uses. microsoft/vscode#327437 is open (a heap snapshot showed ~38 live terminals holding ~80 MB of a 484 MB renderer heap) and coder/code-server#6413 reports browser-tab RAM reaching several GB with a continuous-output terminal left running after the tab is closed; neither has a maintainer mitigation. Closing the tab is the mitigation, and the numbered sessions are what make the live set match the tabs you can see.

GitHub token expired, or the workspace has no GitHub account -> GitHub reauth

  • What you see: git push answers remote: Invalid username or token. Password authentication is not supported for Git operations., or gh auth status calls the token invalid. An expired token and a never-connected account read the same from that message, so ask which one you have before you touch either.
  • What its answers mean here: REJECTED beside env token (GITHUB_TOKEN/GH_TOKEN) is an expired mint (401 refuses the credential itself, which is what an hour-old injected copy is); NO GitHub credential in the chain slot means nothing is connected and nothing can be minted; PUSH-READY means the credential is fine and you want the push-denied entry instead.

It is idempotent and it never prints a token.

Private-repo clone or push denied while a credential is present -> the grant, not the format

  • What you see is one of: remote: Invalid username or token. Password authentication is not supported for Git operations., remote: Repository not found., fatal: Authentication failed for 'https://github.com/...', or fatal: could not read Username for 'https://github.com'. None of them names the token or its age, and the first is what a refused token plus a silent askpass looks like, not anything to do with passwords.
  • The one command, run where the push was attempted, naming the repository:

It does not ask "is there a credential" and it does not trust the environment: it runs git's own configured helper the way git runs it, takes the password that would go on the wire, and probes THAT credential against the endpoint git push negotiates through - one GET of <repo>.git/info/refs?service=git-receive-pack. A read-only credential prints REFUSED-GRANT, never a pass; a healthy-but-shadowed one prints push would FAIL, never ok. Inside a workspace (or the contributor devcontainer) it runs SELF mode with no docker and prints one self: line per credential; on the stack host it enumerates the labeled workspace containers, or probes a named container alone. Flags may go before or after the positionals, and a path below owner/repo is refused rather than probed.

  • The repair is also one command, and every push would FAIL line names it:
  • Read the report by its last line, then by these. git would send this credential (source: <slots>) is the credential a real push uses, in git's consult order; the same token held by several slots is named once, as one credential with several names. A plain credential present (source: <slots>) is a credential that exists and that git never reaches.
  • [shadowed: the credential above outranks this slot, ...] is the most misread line in the report: the credential under it is healthy and git will not use it while the env pair stands. env -u GH_TOKEN -u GITHUB_TOKEN <command> makes git or gh use that slot for one command; fix makes it permanent for git. See the Bad credentials entry.
  • NO GitHub credential in the <slot> slot (git will prompt and be refused) means there is nothing to send, so the account comes first: the reauth entry.
  • The note line, note: GIT_ASKPASS is set but answers no credential, which is what turns a refused token into "Password authentication is not supported for Git operations."; a working credential helper makes it moot, is the second half of the story. The agent env exports GIT_ASKPASS pointing at the coder binary the agent staged under /tmp/coder.<rand>/, and in a measured workspace that binary answered every prompt, and coder gitaskpass itself, with unrecognized subcommand and no output, so git got no answer at all and fell through to prompting. Clearing GH_TOKEN/GITHUB_TOKEN helps only while the helper answers; with a silent helper it changes nothing.
  • push would WORK (the credential git consults writes <repo>) and push would FAIL are the lines to gate on, keyed to the credential git would really send; check exits non-zero on FAIL so a script or an agent can refuse to push on it.
  • The verdicts, and what each one costs you:
  • PUSH-READY (200 advertising refs): a push would negotiate. If the push still fails, the credential is not the failing thing.
  • REFUSED-GRANT (403): that credential authenticates and every write to the repo is denied, which is the push 403.
  • NOT VISIBLE (404): a private repo hidden from it answers 404, and so does an absent one; clone and push would both fail.
  • REJECTED (401): github.com refused the credential itself, as it refuses an expired or revoked token - the fate of the injected pair about an hour after start. fix re-mints.
  • no useful answer: github.com gave nothing useful (offline? probe again). A 200 that does not advertise refs is this verdict too: a push is not proven.
  • --source=chain (the default) probes every credential that could answer for that repository; --source=env, --source=gh or --source=mint answers one slot and says beside the answer that git and gh consult the env pair first.
  • Reads prove nothing about push, so nothing here asks a read question: a public repo answers a read for any authenticated caller, so a credential that READS a repo can still be refused every WRITE to it. Go to the GitHub side only after the report says REFUSED-GRANT or NOT VISIBLE.
  • The grant behind the credential - the GitHub App installation that the External Auth

    External Auth

    Coder's GitHub OAuth login, the only GitHub credential this stack provisions.

     provider (id github by default) minted its token from - has to include the repository the workspace clones or pushes: GitHub -> Settings -> Applications -> <app> -> Configure -> Repository access.
  • An empty github.com/settings/apps page is the usual surprise here: it means no App is installed under your account, so there is no Configure link to click and nothing to grant, while the provider itself stays configured and keeps minting tokens that authenticate. Install Coder

    Coder

    The control plane: provisions one Docker container per workspace over the host Docker socket.

    's App from the workspace Install GitHub App button, or at github.com/apps/coder/installations/new, grant the repo, then restart. A private repository is never visible to a credential that was never granted it.
  • Then check the URL scheme, which no probe can fix: that credential covers https://github.com/... remotes only, so a git@github.com: or ssh:// URL gets neither helper nor askpass token and needs an SSH key you placed yourself, which this stack provisions nowhere.
  • Then check how the credential is sent, because the two GitHub endpoints disagree about the scheme. api.github.com and gh accept Authorization: Bearer <token>. The git data endpoint refuses it: one token answered /user with 200 and <repo>.git/info/refs?service=git-receive-pack with 401 plus remote: invalid credentials while the token rode a bearer header. git has to send it as Basic auth with the token as the password. The username text is not checked (measured on Coder

    Coder

    The control plane: provisions one Docker container per workspace over the host Docker socket.

     v2.36.6: toxicoder, x-access-token, somebody-else and octocat each returned 200), but an empty username or an empty password is refused, and the empty password is what produces the misleading Invalid username or token. Password authentication is not supported for Git operations.
  • Do not hand-roll a credential helper. Measured across 222 past sessions in this workspace: 29 hit a GitHub auth error (Bad credentials 19, Password authentication is not supported 11, could not read Username 5, unrecognized subcommand 4), and agents hand-rolled their own askpass scripts in 5 sessions and hand-edited credential.helper in 4. Both were wrong the same way: they fought the credential-helper precedence that fix repairs, and they put a live token where ps could read it, while the line that names the real cause was one check away. fix is idempotent, keeps every token off argv and out of any file it creates, and repairs the helper plus the store it reads.
  • Your own credential stays gated on the report: install one only after check has answered REFUSED-GRANT, NOT VISIBLE or REJECTED. No verdict short of those justifies a pasted token, and the repo rule is that a workspace's GitHub credential comes from the External Auth

    External Auth

    Coder's GitHub OAuth login, the only GitHub credential this stack provisions.

     provider alone. From the stack host (it drives docker exec, so it has no SELF path), on stdin:

It installs that credential into that one workspace's gh auth store and then re-installs the env-proof helper that gh auth setup-git would otherwise leave behind, since that helper goes straight back to echoing a stale env pair over the token just pasted. A PAT is never typed as an argument: argv is readable through ps and the token lands in shell history. Pipe it in (echo "$TOKEN" | bazelisk run //scripts:github-auth -- auth <container> -) or run auth <container> alone and answer the hidden prompt. In the line above, - is the only argument after the container and < PAT is a shell redirect, not an argument. It REPLACES the per-start minted credential for that workspace, and while the account stays connected the next gh_token_refresh run rewrites the store, so treat a pasted PAT as a stand-in and rotate or remove it in GitHub -> Applications when the work ends.

  • Full usage, verdict kinds and both argument orders: bazelisk run //scripts:github-auth -- -h.

gh answers Bad credentials -> the stale env pair, not the store

  • What you see, inside a workspace: gh api /user, gh pr create or gh repo view answers Bad credentials (HTTP 401) while the same command on the stack host works, and gh auth status still insists you are logged in. This is the most frequent GitHub failure here: 19 of 222 past sessions in this workspace hit Bad credentials.
  • Cause: Coder

    Coder

    The control plane: provisions one Docker container per workspace over the host Docker socket.

     injects GH_TOKEN/GITHUB_TOKEN into the agent environment when the workspace starts. That GitHub App user-to-server token expires about an hour later and the injected copy is never refreshed for the life of the workspace. gh consults that pair before it reads its own auth store, so it sends the dead token while the store beside it, re-minted by the gh_token_refresh coder_script, is healthy and unreachable.
  • The answer for every gh call, for as long as that workspace lives:

No process can rewrite another process's environment, so the stale pair stays in the environment until the workspace restarts; the prefix is the permanent form, not a workaround you graduate from.

  • git needs no prefix once fix has run, because the helper it installs clears the pair itself:
  • You read the right line when check marks the healthy stored credential [shadowed: ...]: that label is this entry. If the credential check says git would send is the env token and it answers REJECTED, fix is the repair; if it answers REFUSED-GRANT, it is a grant and the clicks are in the push-denied entry.

gh: command not found inside a workspace -> the helper needs gh

  • What you see is gh: command not found, or fix refusing with cannot install the credential helper - gh is not installed in this environment; install gh (apt install gh, or the pinned copy the golden image ships) and run this again. check reports the same hole honestly: with no gh there is no gh stored login slot to read, and a chain with nothing else in it prints NO GitHub credential.
  • Why it blocks the repair rather than just the CLI: the helper fix installs is gh auth git-credential wrapped in env -u GH_TOKEN -u GITHUB_TOKEN ..., and the credential it points git at is the gh auth store. With no gh binary there is no env-proof helper to install and no store to write, so fix refuses and says so instead of leaving a half-repaired ~/.gitconfig behind.
  • Install gh, then run fix again. The golden image

    golden image

    evo-t1-dev:latest, the image every workspace container is created from.

     ships a pinned copy (gh 2.101.0, from the release tarball, at /usr/local/bin/gh); apt's gh is 2.45 and predates subcommands the agent experience uses, so the durable fix is the image, not the distro package. Rebuild the image, then rebuild the workspace: the image is fixed at create time.
  • Whether you are looking at a missing tool or a missing credential, check is what tells them apart: a missing binary shows up as a slot that cannot answer, a missing grant shows up as REFUSED-GRANT.

Secrets vault (Infisical)

None of this appears on a stack that never adopted the vault: every line below needs INFISICAL_ENABLED truthy in .env, and a verb that needs the vault answers note: <verb> refused: INFISICAL_ENABLED is off. Set INFISICAL_ENABLED=true in .env to adopt the vault, then re-run. (scripts/infisical.sh:230). The flag, the twelve managed keys, the three containers and the operator CLI are operate/secrets.md; what is here is the text you actually see when something in that path does not answer.

the env file was not refreshed from Infisical -> the vault did not answer the bring-up refresh

  • What you see is one warning between -> vault: refreshing the env file from Infisical and -> compose up, printed by scripts/dev-stack.sh:681 and its prod twin scripts/prod-stack.sh:657 (${vault_env} there is the env file that project reads, so the checkout's .env on a default run):
  • Cause: that refresh is best-effort on purpose. With the flag on, up pulls the managed keys into the very file compose is about to interpolate (scripts/dev-stack.sh:677-683), and a vault that cannot be reached must not hold the stack down - so a failed pull costs one warning and the bring-up continues on the credentials the file already held. The reason sits directly above it (scripts/lib/infisical.sh:984-992): error: the Infisical export failed; <file> is untouched when the CLI could not reach the vault, warning: the Infisical export produced an empty file; <file> is untouched when it answered with nothing, or note: the pull was refused before it ran; <file> keeps the values it has when a required key is still empty.
  • Nothing is broken yet and nothing repairs itself by waiting: the stack is up, on values the vault may no longer hold. Ask the vault and the inventory first - check is a diagnostic and always exits 0:
  • Each answer is one line: note: <KEY> is empty; set it in <file> before this verb can reach the vault per key that is not filled (scripts/infisical.sh:215), note: no Infisical CLI installed; run: bazelisk run //scripts:infisical -- install-cli when the binary is what is missing (scripts/infisical.sh:346), and warning: the machine identity could not exchange a token; check the client id and secret, and that the vault answers when the vault is there but will not authenticate the identity (scripts/infisical.sh:361). Then retry the pull and bring the stack up again, because compose reads the file only when it recreates a container (scripts/infisical.sh:527):

infisical: vault not configured for this stack -> the boot fetch ran with an empty name on the agent environment

  • The line is in the workspace start log, in the script Coder

    Coder

    The control plane: provisions one Docker container per workspace over the host Docker socket.

     labels Fetch stack secrets from Infisical (templates/workspace/main.tf:723, same body in the devcontainer twin at templates/devcontainer/main.tf:774):
  • Cause: the body's first gate, templates/common/infisical-secrets.sh.tftpl:14-20 - any one of those six empty on the agent environment prints this and exits 0, so the workspace boots with no vault secrets and nothing else complains. The resource exists at all only while infisical_enabled is true (templates/workspace/main.tf:721), so this is not the flag being off; it is one value that never arrived. The push forwards each of the five read-side values only when .env carries something real - env_get_forwardable drops an empty value and one still spelling change-me* (scripts/push-template.sh:198-205, the five forwards at :696-730) - and the template variable then keeps its own empty default (templates/workspace/coder.tf:223-227), which hands the boot body a key that is present and empty.
  • Fix it on the stack host: fill the five read-side keys (INFISICAL_PROJECT_ID, INFISICAL_MACHINE_IDENTITY_ID, INFISICAL_ENVIRONMENT, INFISICAL_UNIVERSAL_AUTH_CLIENT_ID, INFISICAL_UNIVERSAL_AUTH_CLIENT_SECRET) in .env. The sixth name, INFISICAL_DOMAIN, is the one the push composes, so it is empty only when the flag itself is off; INFISICAL_URL is the host CLI's own origin and reaches no workspace. Then read back what still counts as empty and push the template again:

  • Then restart the workspace. The six are agent environment values Coder

    Coder

    The control plane: provisions one Docker container per workspace over the host Docker socket.

     renders per start (templates/workspace/main.tf:549, :639-653) and the body is run_on_start (:720), so a running workspace keeps the empty set until it starts again.

  • The push prints only the key each value came from, never the value (scripts/push-template.sh:696-700), so a CI log that shows infisical_project_id passed from INFISICAL_PROJECT_ID in .env (value not shown) proves the key was read, not that it was right. check is the read that answers. The instance URL is the one vault value the log does print, because the push composes it rather than forwarding it: a workspace is handed http://host.docker.internal:<INFISICAL_PORT> (scripts/push-template.sh:652-661), never the host's own INFISICAL_URL.

infisical: pull-on-start is off (INFISICAL_PULL_ON_START) -> this boot never dials the vault, which is the shipped state

  • Same script, one line, and it is a note rather than a fault:
  • Cause: the body's second gate, templates/common/infisical-secrets.sh.tftpl:27-30. Each twin declares infisical_pull_on_start with default = false (templates/workspace/coder.tf:270-274, templates/devcontainer/coder.tf:257-261), and the push forwards --var infisical_pull_on_start=true only when .env carries a truthy INFISICAL_PULL_ON_START under a truthy INFISICAL_ENABLED (scripts/push-template.sh:636, :668-671), so an adopted vault still ships a boot that never waits on the network. That off is the safe side of a real trade: a fetch that reaches the vault is a fetch bounded by the script's own timeout = 120 (templates/workspace/main.tf:730), and the exit is 0 either way because no secret manager gets to fail a workspace start.
  • What the boot keeps is whatever ~/.infisical/agent.env an earlier start wrote, which on a workspace that has never pulled is nothing at all. To load the credentials now, on the stack host:
  • That writes the stack's env file, not the workspace's. For the workspace's own copy, set INFISICAL_PULL_ON_START=true in .env, re-push, and restart - every later start then fetches, and the note stops printing:

infisical: refused to publish <home>/.infisical/agent.env; the staged file names a shell-control variable -> the belt fired, not the filter

  • The line is the workspace's, from the same script, and the path is that home directory (templates/common/infisical-secrets.sh.tftpl:238-243):
  • Cause: after the publish loop the body reads the staged file once more against one alternation built from its own deny list, and a match deletes the staged file, prints that, and exits 0 - it refuses rather than correcting, and the agent.env an earlier boot wrote stays exactly as it was. That is why the workspace keeps working, and why the line names neither a key nor a value.
  • This is the belt, not the filter. The loop already drops every deny-listed name before a line is staged (templates/common/infisical-secrets.sh.tftpl:181-189), compared upper-cased so BASH_ENV, bash_env and Bash_Env fall in one arm, and the body's own comment reserves the second pass for a filter that regressed or a staged file edited by hand (templates/common/infisical-secrets.sh.tftpl:219-229). A vault key that is simply on that list is therefore not this entry: it disappears from agent.env with no line at all, which is the quiet path.
  • Cost of the refusal is one refresh - unlike the loop's filter, which would have cost the workspace an unset PATH HOME IFS line had the body appended one instead (templates/common/infisical-secrets.sh.tftpl:225-229). Clear whatever wrote to the staged file, prove the vault answers from the stack host, and restart the workspace to run the fetch again:

infisical: skipped a secret whose value spans more than one line -> the vault holds a multi-line secret

  • One line per boot, whatever the number of such secrets, and it names neither the key nor the value (templates/common/infisical-secrets.sh.tftpl:200-204):
  • Cause: the body publishes single-line values only (templates/common/infisical-secrets.sh.tftpl:190-209). A value that opens a single quote without closing it on the same line is a multi-line secret - a PEM, say - and its continuation lines would be republished as keys of their own, which corrupts the value and puts secret bytes into key names. So the whole entry goes, including every line up to the one that closes the quote (:146-153). The vault stores such a value happily; only the workspace publish drops it, and the host-side pull of the twelve managed keys is a different path that never passes through this loop (scripts/lib/infisical.sh:958-1017).
  • Nothing prints which key, on purpose, so the shape to look for is the secret you added most recently that is not one line - a private key or a certificate. Either store it as one line (base64 of the PEM is the usual form) or keep it host-side, then restart the workspace to fetch again.
  • The drop is a stated boundary rather than a bug: see the No multi-line value reaches a workspace bullet in operate/secrets.md.

The hermes vhost is not typed by hand: STACK_ROUTER_CONF in .env names the conf compose mounts (proxy/router.gen.conf, which bootstrap renders from proxy/router.conf.template, or the checked-in proxy/router.conf while that key is empty), and every server_name in it is composed from the naming parts. Under STACK_PUBLIC_HOSTS=auto a missing or mistyped part is what produces a name nothing answers. Traefik

Observability

The ten profile-gated services (prometheus, mimir, loki, tempo, grafana, alloy, node_exporter, cadvisor, blackbox_exporter, alertmanager) fail quietly, because a monitoring stack that stopped collecting still answers /ready. The shape of every entry below is the same: the read path (Grafana) and the write path (Prometheus -> Mimir, Alloy -> Loki) are separate, so decide which side is empty before you touch either. What each piece is for and where its config lives is in observability.md.

An Observability card reads DOWN while the container is up -> the badge probes an endpoint, not a process

Cause: the card's siteMonitor is a specific path (/api/health, /-/healthy, /ready), and "the container exists" says nothing about that path answering. Four of the six containers are distroless, so nothing inside them can be asked; the log is the only interrogation available.

Use the name that failed, and dev-stack for the dev project. A service that restarts into the same failure has usually been handed a config file it rejects - observability/loki/loki.yml and its three siblings are bind-mounted read-only, so the file in the checkout is the file that failed, and git diff names what changed.

The other cause is that the service genuinely is not ready: Mimir, Loki and Tempo report /ready only once their ingester is, so a badge that goes down under load is a real signal, not a stale card.

Prometheus shows no target for a service -> the scrape list, the /metrics path, or the bearer

Cause: "no target" and "one target, down" are different faults. Check which one you have from the stack host:

  • Absent from the list entirely: the job is not in observability/prometheus/prometheus.yml. Add it there and let the collector read it again: that file arrives through a bind mount, which follows the path, so the edit is already inside the container and only the running process is behind it. Restarting the service picks it up, and POST /-/reload answers 200 on this one (--web.enable-lifecycle, docker-compose.yml:854) without dropping the scrape loop's in-flight state. A recreate is what you need when the mount line or another compose setting changed, not for an edit to a file that is already mounted.
  • Present and down: the app is not answering on the name Prometheus dials. The scrapes are compose-DNS (coder:2112, litellm:4000), not the host mappings - a curl 127.0.0.1:2112 that works from the host proves only that the port mapping is fine.
  • litellm alone is down with a 401: the scrape sends the master key as a bearer token that it reads from a file, /etc/prometheus-secrets/litellm_token (observability/prometheus/prometheus.yml), which Compose writes from LITELLM_MASTER_KEY when it creates the container. Measured on v3.16.0, the collector expands environment variables under global.external_labels - they come back filled in at /api/v1/status/config - and nowhere a credential could hide: a scrape target address and an authorization block send the written text back verbatim, so a value it could not substitute is rejected. That file is the one credential in the bundle a rotate can strand, and it behaves the opposite way from the bind mounts above: it is a Compose configs entry, and Compose writes those when it creates the container. Measured with the compose this repo ships, up -d after a rotate prints Running, keeps the same container and the same com.docker.compose.config-hash, and the file inside still holds the old key; a restart matches it. The recreate that works names the service - docker compose -p evo-t1-prod --profile observability -f docker-compose.yml up -d --force-recreate prometheus, the invocation prod-stack itself prints with the recreate added, since prod-stack up passes no flags through. The response body names the fault: LiteLLM

    LiteLLM

    The single OpenAI-compatible proxy in front of every model, local and remote.

     answers a missing bearer with "Malformed API Key passed in", and a wrong one with No connected db. - which is an auth failure at v1.102.1, not a database complaint (this bundle runs LiteLLM

    LiteLLM

    The single OpenAI-compatible proxy in front of every model, local and remote.

     with no DB at all). bazelisk run //scripts:observability-check prints that target's lastError, so it names the 401 without a docker logs read.

Grafana's dashboard page logs a quotas 501 and skipping rendering -> two separate upstream lines, one of them closed here

Cause: both show up in the browser console on every dashboard page, and only one of them means anything.

  • GET /apis/quotas.grafana.app/v0alpha1/namespaces/default/usage?group=dashboard.grafana.app&resource=dashboards answering 501 (Not Implemented) is upstream grafana/grafana#136271: with unified_storage.overrides_path unset the resource server's quota service is nil and refuses the call, while the browse-dashboards view fires it on every page load. This bundle closes it by pointing Grafana at observability/grafana/unified-storage/overrides.yml through GF_UNIFIED_STORAGE_OVERRIDES_PATH, so the call answers 200. The file sets no limit; its presence is the whole fix, and what the endpoint then reports is Grafana's own default - {"usage":0,"limit":1000} for both dashboards and folders on grafana/grafana:13.3.1. No cap is known to take effect there: four plausible shapes written under overrides: left that 1000 untouched, and three other shapes stop the container at boot, so the file's own header says to prove a limit on the pinned image before committing one. If the 501 is back, the bind or the variable went missing - and the knob cuts both ways: pointed at a path that is not there, Grafana does not fall back to the 501, it exits 1 with Error: overrides file does not exist (measured on 13.3.1), and restart: unless-stopped loops it. A missing bind source makes that shape on its own, since Docker mounts a directory where the file should be, so a checkout that never got observability/grafana/unified-storage/overrides.yml costs the whole dashboard rather than one console line.
  • DashboardScenePage.tsx:171 skipping rendering is a leftover console.log in Grafana's own bundle (public/app/features/dashboard-scene/pages/DashboardScenePage.tsx, read out of the pinned image's source map). It prints when the page declines to render for one pass because the route's dashboard uid changed under it, which is the normal path for any navigation between dashboards and for a trip to or from Home. It carries no diagnostic value, shares no cause with the 501, and keeps printing after that one is fixed. Nothing in this stack can silence it, and nothing needs to.

So a console that shows only skipping rendering is a healthy Grafana, and a panel that is empty is not this line's fault - take the datasource path below.

Grafana's datasource tests green but the panel is empty -> the Mimir query path, then the tenancy header

Cause: the mimir datasource is http://mimir:8080/prometheus, and that suffix is Mimir's Prometheus-compatible query namespace - not its root and not its write endpoint. /api/v1 on its own is the write-side namespace and answers 404 to a query_range, so a datasource pointed there still reads green in the UI and returns nothing in a panel. That URL is the single most common cause of this symptom.

Work it in this order:

  1. Run the same query in Explore against the prometheus datasource and then the mimir one, over the same range. Data in one and not the other is a write-path fault, not a dashboard fault.

  2. Data in prometheus and none in mimir: read what the write did.

    A refused or failing remote_write (target http://mimir:8080/api/v1/push) shows up here, and an ingester that refuses a block shows up in bazelisk run //scripts:prod-stack -- logs --tail 200 mimir.

  3. Nothing anywhere: the scrape is the fault, so take the target entry above.

  4. Only then look at tenancy. Mimir is multi-tenant by design and keeps tenancy on until a config says otherwise; once it is on, every read and every write must carry an X-Scope-OrgID header or be refused. This stack turns it off with multitenancy_enabled: false in observability/mimir/mimir.yml, so the provisioned datasource sends no tenancy header and the compose network is the trust boundary. A query that starts insisting on a header means that file changed, not that the data went missing - and re-enabling tenancy is a change to the remote_write credentials as well, not just to Grafana.

The shipped datasources carry fixed UIDs (prometheus, mimir, loki, tempo) that every shipped dashboard references, so a datasource you rebuilt by hand in the UI is a datasource no panel will ever query. Diff anything suspicious against observability/grafana/provisioning/datasources/stack.yaml: that file is the record of what the working config is.

Alloy ships no logs and Loki stays empty -> the host's log root is not STACK_DOCKER_LOG_DIR

Cause: the only host path in the bundle is ${STACK_DOCKER_LOG_DIR:-/var/lib/docker/containers}, mounted read-only into Alloy. If the daemon writes its json-file logs somewhere else, Alloy tails an empty directory and Loki's badge stays green, because /ready reports the store, not the supply.

Check the source path on the stack host, where the daemon actually is (inside a workspace docker addresses that workspace's own sidecar, so the answer you get is about the wrong daemon):

No *-json.log files there means the daemon has a different --data-root. Rootless Docker is the usual case - it keeps them under the user's own state directory (~/.local/share/docker/containers) - and a daemon started with an explicit --data-root is the other. Name the real one in the env file that belongs to that stack and recreate the service:

The second cause is the logging driver: a container not using json-file has no such file to tail, so its logs are missing from Loki while every other service's arrive. The collector's own log names which files it opened:

The traces dashboard is empty and Tempo logs a 404 once a minute -> Prometheus has no write receiver

Cause: Tempo's metrics_generator does not expose span-metrics for Prometheus to scrape. It computes them and remote_writes them to http://prometheus:9090/api/v1/write, and Prometheus answers that with 404 remote write receiver needs to be enabled with --web.enable-remote-write-receiver until the flag is on. The service is healthy either way, so the only visible symptom is a tracing dashboard with no series and a Tempo log that repeats msg="non-recoverable error" ... failedSampleCount once a flush interval.

The flag is on the Prometheus command in docker-compose.yml. Confirm it survived, then confirm the series arrived:

An empty data with the flag present and no Tempo error means nothing is producing spans yet. Grafana is the one shipped client (GF_TRACING_ENABLED), so drive a few requests through the Grafana API and check again; a traces_spanmetrics_calls_total series with a service_name is the proof the whole path works.

Public grafana-gmktecbeast answers 421 -> the name composed, the container did not

Cause: the same 421 the Hermes

Hermes

The Nous Research host assistant, with the Web Dashboard and its approval prompts.

 entry above describes - this box's router answers it when the Host matches no server_name - with one extra way to reach it that the other five names do not have. scripts/lib/domain.sh composes the Grafana name from the naming parts and reads no flag, so bootstrap writes the vhost and STACK_GRAFANA_URL even when OBSERVABILITY_ENABLED=false. The router then has a correct server_name with nothing behind it, and the browser gets a 502 from Traefik

Traefik

The reverse proxy that terminates TLS for the public names.

 or a 421 if the Host was rewritten before it arrived.

Work it in this order:

  1. Is the container there at all? A name with no container is the flag, not the router.

  2. Does the router carry the vhost? STACK_ROUTER_CONF in .env decides which conf compose mounts, so a rendered proxy/router.gen.conf that predates the Grafana naming has no grafana block in it. Re-run bazelisk run //scripts:bootstrap and compare.

  3. Is Traefik

    Traefik

    The reverse proxy that terminates TLS for the public names.

     aimed at the router and not at :3005? The public path is Traefik

    Traefik

    The reverse proxy that terminates TLS for the public names.

     -> router :8080 -> grafana:3000; a backend that points straight at the container never reads the vhost file and Grafana answers with its own 404.

  4. Is Grafana behind a login you have not supplied? GF_AUTH_ANONYMOUS_ENABLED is false in this stack, so an unauthenticated probe is redirected to /login and a monitoring check that treats a redirect as a failure reports the UI as down.

dev-stack status says running, never healthy -> those four images have no shell

Cause: by design. Only prometheus and grafana declare a healthcheck, because grafana/mimir, grafana/loki, grafana/tempo and grafana/alloy are distroless - no shell, no wget, no curl - so any command a healthcheck ran would fail in the image rather than on the service. running is the best state those four can report, and adding a healthcheck to one of them is not the fix for an anxious operator.

Prove liveness the way the stack does: the Observability cards on the dashboard (http://loki:3100/ready, http://tempo:3200/ready, http://mimir:8080/ready over compose DNS), or a datasource's Test button in Grafana. Those three publish no host port, so there is no host-side curl to fall back to, and docker compose exec cannot help either - there is nothing to exec into. The container log is the last word:

The six never come up after setting the flag -> which env file that project reads

Cause: OBSERVABILITY_ENABLED is read from the environment the compose command runs with, and each project reads a different file. dev-stack passes --env-file dev-stack.env when that file sits beside the compose file, so a dev run never sees .env; prod-stack names no env file unless -e does, and compose then reads .env beside the compose file. Setting the key in the wrong one changes nothing.

Ten rows when the profile is selected, none when it is not. With the flag off the five Observability cards on the dashboard read down together, which is the honest signal rather than a card bug: the badge reports what each endpoint answers, and the flag is the reason none of them answer. Then:

  • A value of false, 0, no or off turns the bundle off; anything else turns it on. One helper decides, compose_observability_args in scripts/lib/common.sh, so the runners (dev-stack, prod-stack, update-stack) cannot disagree with each other.
  • A hand-typed docker compose ... up -d selects no profile at all, flag or not - profiles are per command, which is exactly what the runners add. A service the profile did create also keeps running after the flag goes off until you stop it.
  • Both paths parse or the build fails: bazelisk run //scripts:validate runs docker compose config -q once plain and once with --profile observability.
  • Turning the flag on needs the payload tree, not just the flag: the six bind mounts read observability/**, so a checkout that has docker-compose.yml ahead of the observability/ directory (a partial pull) fails mounting, the same failure shape as the missing bind-mount source at the top of this page.
